A LUCKY BABY.

Though the fact that she is a girl has greatly lessened the importance of the baby who was born to the Duke and Duchess of Norfolk the other day, the little person is noverthel-ss one of the most important babies of the year, for not only, of course, is she the daughter of the premier Duke in England, but she is heiress in her own right to the Barony of Herries, and in due time will be a great heiress who may be expected to make a great marriage. Her adven must be a great joy to the Duke of Norfolk, who is passionately fond of children.

div.head: TRAINING YOUNG SERVANTS.
div.p: TRAINING YOUNG SERVANTS.

A careful article on "The Training of Young Servants" recently appeared in the Women's pages of the Guardian. It is signed "F. G.," but the chief point of interest, writes "Lorna" in the British Weekly, is not mentioned, namely, that the writer herself, as I happen to know, has been for many years in domestic service. She speaks from experience when she says: "The mistress who knows how to rule will nearly always be well served. The unpopularity of what ought to be, and is, the most desirable occupation for working-class women of the best type is due in no small measure to the incapables of both ranks." "F. G." pleads for a thorough technical education for domestic service.

div.head: WHITE Curra Conran.
div.p: WHITE Curra Conran.

White gowns of every description are enjoying a tremendous vogue this season. Our illustration shews a smart and novel costume achieved in thin white cloth. The little cape-coatee consists of three shaped capes fitting closely to the curve of the figure, and thence falling in slight, graceful folds. The fronts of this coat are held together by four wide straps of cloth, which also hold in place the fulness of a creamy lace iabot. The sleeves are of three-

quarter length, and are slit up for some little way to admit of the insertion of a small lace frill. The graceful skirt is of the corselet shape—belt and skirt cut in one—the immense width of the tucked skirt being shaped out in two stitched seama on each side. Above this skirt is worn a lace blouse, of which the jabot forms part. The hat worn with this costume is of white Tagal straw, trimmed with turquoise velvet and snowy wings.

div.head: PRINCESS FREDERICA'S PEARLS.
div.p: PRINCESS FREDERICA'S PEARLS.

There is a romantic story attaching to the great rope of pearls worn by the Princess Frederica of Hanover at recent function, says the Tat/e. They are magnificent specimens, and very old. Centuries ago a princess of the house loved them so that they were buried with her. But in process of time the great grief of her relatives grew gradually fainter and fainter, until they began to whisper what a shame it was that such glorious jewels should be so wasted. Then one day the princess's tomb was opened and the pearl necklace taken from her neck. But the pearls were ,poilt; they had lost their lustre and beauty. Their new owner wept over them and dreamt about them, and her dream told her that three generations of lovely women would have to wear them before their lustre returned. Three lovely princesses did wear them, and they are now pearls without peers.

Gums' Waoscs.

Whatever a girl does it seems inevitable. says Edith Thompson in Cassell's Magazine, that she should be laughed at, and she must learn to ex- pect this. A few years ago she was called a "bluestocking" for her devotion to learning; next an "empty-headed, overdressed doll ''•, and now she is • a creature of iron muscles, of waistless symmetry, of biceps and ungainliness." Should she turn her energies to cooking and domesticity, she becomes a "mere household drudge." _

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Society's Autumn Arrangements.—The King and Queen are to be the guests oi the Duke of Richmond at Goodwood House during the racing. Last year the Duke, owing to family, mourning, placed G )odwood House at the disposal of their Majesties, but on this occasion he will be present as the host. Goodwood and tjse Regatta week at Cowes, are the remaining events before the general separation for the autumn holidays, which as usual, will be spent by several members of the Royal Family' and many of the great people in Society in 'Scotland. The visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales to India, will induce a larger number than usual to join parties bent upon Eastern travel, but everything promises well for the Highland season in Scotland. The Prince and Princess will not he away for so long as when they visited Australia, and their chiidren willespend the autumn in Scotland. The two elder Princes are to be brought up for the sea, thus following in the footsteps of their father. They are not to go to a public school, but will remain for the present under their tutor, Mr. Hansel I, and will eventually go to Osborne, or one of the cadet ships for naval training, Royal and Other Golfers.—There are golf links at Windsor, Sandringham, and Balmoral, but the game is not one which is much favoured by members of the Itoyal Family. Among them, the Duchess of Connaught is almost alone in being particularly keen on the game, and it was whilst on a visit to Lord and Lady Dudley at Witley Court, that she became a convert to its fascinations. Lord Dudley is a great golfer, an be has a first rate course at his Worcestershire seat, Witley Court. There are also private links at the Viceregal Lodge. upon which he plays a good deal when in Dublin. The Duke of Portland, Lord and Lady Cadogan, Lord Dunraven, and Lady Barrington, are among others who have private golf links at their country houses, but the best of all is the private course at Chatsworth, the Duke of Devonshire who is a keen golfer, having spared neither trouble or expense in maleing it perfect. The Double Wedding of the Queen's Maids.—lt was =carding to the Queen's wish that the weddings of her two maids of honour, the Hon. Dorothy Vivian and the Hon. Mary Dyke, should take place together in the private chapel at Buckingham Palace this week. Itwas the first occasion upon which a wedding other than that of a member of the Royal family. has taken place at the Palace, and only two Royal marriages have been solem- nized there—those of Princess Louise to the Duke of Fife, and Princess Maud to Prince Charles of Denmark. The chapel is very small and consequently the King and Queen, together with other members of the Royal family, and only near relations of the brides and bride- grooms, were present at the double wedding of the Queen's maids. The marriage of the Hon. eery Dyke to Major Bell was not to have taken place until the end of July. hut at the Queen's suggestion, it was altered so as to synchronize with the wedding of the Hon. Dorothy , Vivian and Major Douglas Hay. Miss Vivian's engage- ment was of a somewhat romantic character, as she only met her husband for the first time during the recent visit of the King of Spain to this country. Women who have the Gift of Oratory.—ThZi Duchess of Marlborough has been very busy during the season with various social schemes and entertainments in the cause of charity. She is richly endowed with the art of oratory, a gift which enables her to preside at the opening of a bazaar, or a distribution of prizes with perfect ease and grace. Some of her ability in this respect is no doubt due to hersernerican birth and train- ing, though she by no means stands alone among the women who are excellent public speakers. Lady Warwick, and her sister the Duchess of Sutherland, both have the gift of oratory to an unusual degree, and so also have Lady Jersey, Lady Frederick Cavendish, and Lady Carlise. The Wealth of Words.—Tt seems astonishing to hear that ordinary well-educated people use no more than 3,000 or 4,000 words in conversation. Yet this is stated in one of the July magazines to be the case, whilst it is , added that the most eloquent speakers seldom if ever exceed a vocabulary of 10,000 words. If this is a fact, it would appear that there must be a vast number of words in the English languageeas to which we could well do without. The nee, Oxford Dictionary will, when completed contain a quarter of a million word', yet we are told that the Bible, which may be taken as sin example of perfect expression,contains no more than *3,000 words. Shekespere is credited with employing about 15.000, whilst Milton's works are built up with 3,000. There is not of course the same poverty of language as was the case before the days of popular education, but it is stated on the same authority that there are people in country parishes, who menage to get through life with the usage of not more than 300 Of 400 words. Concerning Motor Hats.—lt has been said that the motor defies the skill of the milliner, but , although this statement is, to a consider : able degree correct, it is an findisputable fact that the feminine motorist is no longer the fearsome object she once was. The new motor hats of soft silky looking linen, and which take the form of a French sailor are delightfully light,and really becoming,and the favourite colour is a dark iron grey, which never shows dust. Veils of ninon are being worn with these hats, and carefully arranged they thoroughly protect the hair. Our Effective covering.—For enveloping an airy-fairy bat or toque, that perchance has to appear at a luncheon party, or an afternoon reception, and must therefore be protected from the crushing process, as well as the dust Reed, shot taffetas hoods, built somewhat after the fashion of those donned by our great grandmothors, are being offered us. These hoods are well wired, and the fair mororiet has therefore no cause for anxiety, even when the most upstanding wines, flowers or feathers, are concerned. A pretty and becoming ruche finishes them oft round the face. Motor Coats.--Ileavy corded silk, taffetas, or tweed, have taken the place of fur or leather for summer motor coats, and these are built in divers styles, from the most elaborate and fussy, and the severely plain. For the women who has talien seriously to motoring, the latter idea is the best. Furbelows for lone " runs " are always a mistake. For motor bairns white is the usual wear, and their little coats and hoods present far fewer difficulties to modistes, than do those of their elder sisters and mothers. Goggles and Masks.—alany mothers eppear to have s great objection to " disfiguring " their children with goggles, the result being a crop of little sufferers from .eye and eyelid troubles. The oculists report that since motoring became general, the number of child patients ' bas increased enormously, and they are unanimous con- cerning the necessity of providing the little people with adequate eye protection. Careful mothers should also see to it that their girls ere well masked aid veiled, otherwise red, roughened, and weather-beaten skins and a harvest of wrinkles about the eyes, will result. A Toilet Hint.—For keeping the complexion in good condition, the following preparation is excellent. Take one pound of pure lard, and turn it into a jar, which should be placed in a saucepan of boiling water, care being taken that the water never reaches the top. 'When the lard is melted, add four heaped tablespoon- fuls of chopped fresh cabbage, and let the mixture simmer for five or six hours. Strain through muslin, and keep in a covered jar.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 15, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 15, 1905.

William Lipp if he had ever been there. Hi thought for some time and replied in dm negative. Then Holme asked 'if he had an, relations there,•and if so, he ought to go ant visit them, etc., etc. 'Lipp relapsed into a long train or thought, and closed his eyes. Finally, he roused him- self, and admitted that he had a relative, a cousin, to be exact, and that this relative lived, not precisely in London, but in Essex. which was, so to speak, part of London. Lord Harry Quy questioned him kindly about this relative, and Lipp, inspired by the ,compliment of so great a personage being in- terested in his humble belongings and warmed by the food, the fire, and the beer, told slowly and with many pauses the story of his cousin's life. How be had been out to the goldfields for seven yearsr And returned with a com- fortable little pile.. How he had set up as a greengrocer in Gorehaven, and how he had generally prospered, and brought the name of Lipp to a high level. The two young men smiled, but listened altentively to every word with an interest that was not entirelyassumed, and at the end of the narrative Holme care- lessly asked if Lipp had heard from his rela- tive lately. The rustic took a deep draught of beer, and chuckled. • "Not a, week ago," he said, " whoi he asked I to post two letters for him, and one of 'eat to a lady of title, said as 'ow he wanted to play a joke on friends of 'is—lady of title, mark ye—and he said—dainn." William Lipp rose unsteadily to his feet, ; and stood with w;de open mouth. " Well ? " said Holme, who was quivering with excitement. Wboi, he said as 'ow I warn't to tell any- body about the letters in case Lady— damn—" and the man scratched his head. I In spite of the serious importance of the news, the two young mien could not help smiling. Then they adroitly turned the con- versation, and in less than a quarter of an hour William Lipp was asleep. Holme whispered to his friend, and they , rose to their feet. Lord Harry slipped two sovereigns into the pocket of the sleeping man and they left the house with the bag that con- tained their clothes, Then they crossed over to the inn, settled handsomely with the land- lord, brought round the motor from the dilapidated coach-house, and ,in less than half an hour Up W.ithing Jay twenty miles to the north of them, and they were speeding southwards as fast as their car could carry thorn. • It was still dark when they ran down from the undulating hills of western Essex, into the flat country that stretched eastwards to . the sea. A thick blanket of mist lay over the I marshes, and the powerful lamps of the car I showed nothing but a white cloud ahead. They slackened down to the lowest speed, and though they were now on roads of which every turn and bend was well known to them, they did not dare run at a greater pace than eight miles an hour, a• crawl that was only obtained by frequent use Of the brake. IBoth men were thoroughly tired out, for • they had had but one night's sleep in the last three days. Holme sat with his chin sunk on his breast, and only the uncomfortable nature of his, seat prevented him from falling asleep. Lord Harry Quy was forced to keep all his senses on the alert, and his nerves were strung up to such a high pitch that the ac- tivity of his brain overcame the physical fatigue of his body. Every now and then he took hold of his companion's arm with his left hand and shook him violently. At last Holme roused himself. He had neasly fallen off his seat, and he began to be impressed with the danger of his position. He looked at his watch. It was half-past • four. Then he peered round into the ;mist, which hung round them like a curtain on every side. "Where are we, Quy ? " he said, with a yawn. • "We've just passed the bridge over Trum- pion's Creek. I'could see nothing, but I felt the rise and fall of the road." Holme looked behind him. " The fog seems to be lifting," he said, "it looks a bit lighter behind' us." Lord Harry Quy gave a hurried look behind him, and then slightly quickened the speed of the car. As be did so the mist behind turned from dark- ness into a dull orange, and from orange into several fainter shades of yello ie. Then there was the low hissing sound of wheels along the muddy road. • "Take one of the side lamps," Lord Harry Quy called out, "and hold it over the back. Scarcely had Holme done so, when the mist showed like white foam behind them, there was a blinding glare of light in his eyes, some- thing dark swerved suddenly to one side, shot past them, showed for a second in the light of their own lamps, e.nd disappeared into the darkness beyond. In that brief second Lord Harry Quy had seen a gigantic black car, and two crouching figures masked and covered with black leather from head to foot. " Jordison ! " he said, putting the lever down another inch. "He must be mad to drive like that. He was all but in to us, and would have smashed us up ff I hadn't thought of that extra lainp." "If he can drive at that pace," replied Hoime, quietly," we can. I'll take the risk." "And I, too, by gad," said Lord Harry Quy. "Itis a straight road." And he moved the lever front speed to speed till the lights of the great car tore like meteors thioueh the darkness.

div.head: BLACK MOTOR CAR. By J. B. HARRIS BURLAND.
div.p: THE BLACK MOTOR CAR. By J. B. HARRIS BURLAND.
CHAPTER XXIV.
WILLIAM LIPP, OF UP WITHING.:

UP WITHING stands five hundred feet above the level of the sea in the very heart of the Yorksh:re Moors. It consists of two score ottages, a public house, licensed for beer 3rily, a rectory, a church, and four farmhouses. The two young men drove slowly up the single street and stopped outside the public house. The whole village{ turned out to examine the car, and a crowd of school child- -en clustered about it like flies round a sugar usin.

Lord Harry Quy went into the little tap- -oom and was regarded apatheticaay by three stolid looking men, each of whom held a quart mug in his horny hand. " The landlord ? " said • Quy interrogatively. One of the men thumped the table with his empty mug, and in a minute the publican appeared. He was short and broad shoul- dered, with an unintelligent face, which seemed to regard the world with a perpetual scowL jHis eyes brightened at the appear- ance of the new corner. He had seen the motor and knew that it represented money. "I and my friend want to stop a night here," Quy said; "have you a room ? " " Noa," said the man, after a p4u.;e. haven't a room."
IC We
"Can you find me one in the village ? " "Dunno. Maybe I can and maybe I can't."

" Jarge could sleep in the stable," said one of the drinkers meditatively. "Oh, could he," replied the landlord in a surly vcice. "How would you like to sleep in the stable, William Lipp ? " Quy started involuntarily at the name, and glanced swiftly at the man addressed by it. In an instant he saw a possible source of in- formation.

"Perhaps Mr:. Lipp has a room," he said pleasantly. " °CVO a room," the man chuckled, "an' oi'll sleep in the kitchen, if I'ze paid for it." " We'll pay," Quy said, and then, seeing the scowl deepen on the landlord's face, he hastened to add," I suppose we could get our meals here, and you could put up the motor ?" "It'd mean turning out our wagon," said the landlord, "an pour wagon's. just been repainted." We will make it worth your while." " Whnt be doin' in these parts? " the land. lord asked suspiciously. Like the rest of England, he had beard of William Jordison, and the idea was forming in his slo.v brain that possibly the murderer stood before him. "On the way to Scotland," Quy answered, curtly. "Something wrong with the car. II will take us a day to get it right. But give me an answer about accommodation. My name is Lord 'Harry Quy. You needn't—be afrak that I'll run off with your spoons." The magic po.ver of a title made itsel manifest in every face. The landlord bowed obsequiously. "What I can give yer, my lord, is at yes disposal." ' I'll be happy to give yer lordship my room," the yokel chimed in," but perhaps the rector---"

"Your room will do, Mr. Lipp," Quy broke in curtly. "Get us a good square meal ready, landlord, we haven't had anything since breakfast." The landlord started to enume- rate the contents of his larder, but Quy cut him short, and went outside to rejoin who was vainly struggling to keep a dozen small boys from touctiing the machinery of the motor. He briefly told his news. Holme's face flushed with excitement.

"It's a lucky discovery, and may lead to something," be said. "On the other hand, the name may be merely a coincidence, and even if this yokel is some relative of jordison's servant, we may be able to get nothing out of him. Does he look like a rogue.? " " There he is," said Quy, pointing at the man v. ho was slouching out of the inn to make preparation . for the reception of his distin- guished guests. Holme looked at the rugged, inexpressive face and smiled.
" No, he is not a rogue, but dull and unin- telligent. ' Such people are often quite as difficult to get information out of. However, we shall see."

Arthur Holme and Lord Harry Quy slept that night in William I.ipp's humble cottage. The bedroom, which: contained one small and one lar;.! bed, was redolent of soap and furni- ture polish. teA small tire crackled in the tiny grate, and a bowl of anemones was placed on the table by the window. Before they turned in for the night they searched the room thoroughly, but kund nothing. The [next morning they expressed them- selves so delighted with their new quarters that they had decided to stay another night. William Lipp went out to his work at day- break, and while the two young men were having hreakfast at the inn, an old dame hob- bled in from rkext door and made the bed. By the time they returned she had disappear- ed,. and they had the house to themselves:

They went into the single room, half kitchen, half parlour„V,lere Lipp spent such part of his time as he could spare from his work and the public-house. Then they proceeded to- turn the room inside out, making a thorough search for something that would connect the occupant with Jordison's servant. They examined the family bible, searched every inch of the cupboards, opened every drawer and went through its contents, scrutinized every piece of paper that they could lay their hands on, but they found nothing. " I've had enough," said Lord Harry Quy, " and I feel pretty mean about all this busi- ness. Let's wait and have a talk to the fellow this evening. We'll have in beer, and I expect we'll get something out of him. It's more straightforward, anyhow." Holme ilia not reply. He was looking hard at the fire-place. The lire was laid, but it had not been lit. William Lipp could only afford to use coal on Sundays. The water for his breakfast and tea was boiled in the house next door. Hohne looked thoughtfully at the three layers of w,..0d, coal and paper. " ICS cold," said Lord Harry Quy, "shall we light it ? " For reply Holme walked over to the fire- place, and pulled out a piece of grey paper which projected from the bars of the grate. It was an envelope addressed to Mr. William Lipp, Up Withing, Yorkshire. It bore the postmark of Gorehaven, in Essex. Holme looked inside. It was empty. He handed it to Lord Harry, who gave a low whistle of sur- prise. "The scent is getting warm," he said "we must certainly have in that beer to- night. Do you recognise the handwriting ? " " No," replied jlcdnie, "it is probably that of Jordison's servant. It is the scrawl ,of an uneducated man. If it is so, we have an im- portant clue to Jordison's whereabouts. This was posted the day after Lady Agnes's dis- appearance, ergo, Jordison was still in the neightxmrhood, , and, ergo, his hiding place is probably not far from Gorehaven." That evening when William Lipp returned from a wet day's work on the hills, he found the fire lit, a great joint of cold roast beef, a jar of pickles, bread and butter, anti a large plum cake on the table. and two gallons of beer reposing en the stone floor. Lord Harry Quy explained that they did not wish to leave the house that night, and hoped he would join them in sonic supper. By eight o'clock most of the beef had gone, and three quarters of the beer was drunk. Holme produced his tobacco pouch, and the three men sat over the tire and smoked. William Lipp, full and satisfied, blinked lazily. He could hardly grasp the situation. He as only sure of one thing : that he had made one of the best meals of his life, and that he had washed it down satisfactorily with un- limited beer. Holme and Quy had no difficulty in obtain. ing the info% mation they required. They commenced to talk about. London, and asked

div.head: CHAPTER XXVi THE LONG ROAD.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVi THE LONG ROAD.

HOLME set his face grimly, as the great cat shot forward into the fog.. The cold, white mist beat into his face like a stream of liquid ice. He gripped the sides of his steel seat with both hands. For the rest he trusted to Providence. and the keen eyes and firm hands of Lord Harry Quy. Holme was not used to motor cars, and a ride of this sort was calculated to try the nerves of an experienced man. The log and darkness closed in on him like the walls of a vault. The engine throbbed and beat be. neath him like the continual whirr of a loom. The air whistled past his ears like the sharp hiss of a serpent. Behind, and on either side, lay impenetrable blackness. Before him, a patch of muddy road rushing towards him trom a white sea of mist. Lord Harry Quy drove like "a madman, his eyes glued on the brown road and the ridge of grass on either side which marked out his course. He knew the danger that lurked in the darkness but he had no time to think of it. His mind was rivetted on a single object and for that he was prepared to risk everything. As the minutes passed and the miles flashed by him all mental and physical fatigue vanished. He became a machine moving relentlessly onward, one with the pulsing shafts and cylinqers beneath him—a soulless automaton quickened to life by a single breath—the voice of a dead girl crying out to him to slay and spare not. Fast as they drove—ann Lord Harry got every ounce of power out of his engines—they did not come up to the fobject • of their chase. Every moment they expected to sec the lights of Jordison's car, but nothing came to them out of the . white mist ahead. Lord Harry cursed aloud. He began to realise that he was beaten. Since the black car had passed them there had been no turning from the one long straight road. It was quite cer- tain that they had followed the rignt ck.rat Yet Jordison had eluded them. Beyond the park wall. the main road ran straight on to the ferry across the Yoke Fleet, while a bye road skii ted this wall and fermed a connecting link between the old Roman causeway and the London Road. It Was quite clear that Jordison would not attempt to cross the ferry, and Lord Harry Quy steered by the wall on his -right and dashed ' into the narrow lane. A shower of mud and • stones and a jolt that nearly dung both the men from their seats warned him that he Must slow down if he did not wish to rip the tyres off the wheels. He reduced the speed to d arnanhour. Slightly up hill. and in less • miles thirty road than a minute the car emerged from the car- pet of fog that covered the lower ground. The ;noon was shining brightly overhead in a clear sky. Both men peered eagerly ahead. 1 At the top of the slope, half a nab oral, •

bright light flashed for a second find dis- appeared. "We're on his heels" said Holme, " can't you go faster ? " • "Certainly, but there is the risk of breaking down altogether." " We must take the risk," Holme replied : "Jordison has taken it." Lord Harry said nothing, but gradually slipped the car on to the top speed. They could sr- warty now, arid the chiet danger lay in the roughness of the road, which appeared to he made of loose round pebbles and mud. As they shot forward; the stones rattled all round them and the mud spurted up in .a con- tinuous stream. The car had as yet no mud guards fixed on to it. When they reached tha top of the hill they saw a light a, may-ahead of them. ' "He's gaining," muttered Holme. ",He has been going downhill," Lord Harry replied. "Now, hold tight." The car shot down the hill like a stone from a sling. Holme's brain was dizzy with the. roar and rush of the air that swePt past him. He clutched the seat with both hands. He imagined the sensation was like that of falling from a great height. He wondered how his ,companion could keep his seat with both 'hands on the steering wheel. Then he noticed that Lord Harry Quy had strapped himself in with a broad leather belt. He shuddered to think of what would happen if the car were to overturn. But his heart was full of gratitude, and admiration. His friend was risking his life for the sake of a woman who loved another man. It was indeed a miracle that the car was not wrecked in that headlong descent, and the , successful passage of these two short miles of down gradient would have proved a fine advertisement for any makers in the world. !The inachine leapt and crashed down the slope like a living thins. Every now and then it seemed as though all hair wheels were off the ground, arid that it was flying through space. Then there would come a grinding crash and shock, and a shower of mud would fly up beiore them like spray from the bows of a vessel. AS luck would have it, the road .was now almost free from stones. But broad though the car was,it rocked from side to side like a ship in a storm, and it seemed to Holme's inexperienced eye as though every swing of its great iron frame would hurl it over on its side ' into the hedge. The whole descent occupied less than a minute, but 'the sensations of an hour .n ere crowded into that brief space of time. Holine gave a sigh of relief as they neared the broad, white stretch of the London road that ran north and soUth to right angles of them. The light was still visible to the north, and was now less than half a mile ahead. For one brief , motnont Lord Harry shut off the supply of petrOl and applied the brake.. They swung round the corner on two wheels, and shot out on the smooth surface of the road. In a few seconds Lord Harry had worked his engines up to their top speed and the strain on his eyes and mind was at last in, some measure relieved. The moon shone clear on a broad smooth road and the speed was terrific. The journey was luxurious compared to what they had just experienced in the fog, and through the morass of that narrow Lane. :They could now see the black car itself, and the smell of its petrol came back to them. But Lord Harry marvelled at its silence. The throb of his own engines could .be heard at Least a mile away. He realised that if once the moon went behind a Cloud, and if Jor- dison cared to risk putting out his lights, they would have nothing to tolloW but their own instincts, and would have to guess at the probable route Jordison would take. Lord Harry looked up at the sky. A heavy cloud of white vapour was already near the moon. Then he looked at the car ahead. He was gaining on it, and he wondered if he could reach it before the earth was plunged in darkness. • Then suddenly, as though in answer to his thoughts, the lights before him vanished, and he had nothing to follow but the outline of the black car on the white road. Five miles ahead of them the main road branched into two portions, one running •WeSt• wards into Hertfordshire and the other going straight north into Suffolk. If the moon disappeared before Jordison reached this spot it would be impossible to tell which road he had taken. The track of the wheels Would have been visible by daylight, or even if they had been going at a moderate speed, but the ground had been traversed by wagons -during , the day, and the pace at which the car rushed over it, blurred all the marks into one smooth surface of brown mud. They had nothing to follow but the car itself. When that became invisible, they would have to trust to good fortune. But, the big 'grey machine was wresting the. ground inch by inch from Jordison's car. It was Llighter than the enormous mass of steels: and iron which had been put together in the somewhat primitive factory of the Red House. It was clear, too, that something was wrong with the machinery of the black car. In the moonlight Lord Harry Quy could see that the • two occupants were looking for the cause of the trouble, and that one of them was holding a light to the sparking plugs. Holme had no doubt that they would overtake Jordison before twenty minutes had elapsed, and he began to ask himself what would happen if they got alongside of him. Both he and Lord Harry were unarmed, and he realised that they had to do with desperate men., &To be continued.)

div.head: i WARRINGTON AND MR. CARNEGIE. More Criticism of the Suggested "Cadging,"
div.p: i WARRINGTON AND MR. CARNEGIE. More Criticism of the Suggested "Cadging,"

In the current issue of the " Dawn" Mention writes under " Sunrise Notes "as follows :—" The proposal to ask Mr. Andrew Carnegie for the wherewithal to build a new, or to extend the existing, local Librory has not unnaturally met with opposition. Councillor Wright, who worked, it seems, for Mr. Carnegie some years ago, has won an almost national notoriety by his criticisms of the way in which the famous little Scotch American has made his wealth. His opposition may be summed up in the phrase that Mr. Carnegie's mosey " not clean enough for a town like Warrington," and his sub- sequent suggestion that, if we built the Library and placed a table; on it specifying who had given it, we ought to add another picturing the gaunt spectres of misery and suffering whom he had I made. T do not know enough to sit in judgment on Mr. Carnegie's character, and I am rather inclined to think, upon the whole, that, if money be badly earned, it is a sign of grace to spend it well; but I must confess that, all the same, I do not like the idea of going cap in hand to rich Americans (or Scotchmen, if you will) and asking them to do what We are very well able to do ourselves. It savours overmuch of what the Mayor, with his accustomed bluntness, instantly I described as "cadging;" and lam glad to know that 1 the Museum Committee itself was norunanimous on I the matter, and that even those who voted for the pro posal did so mainly because of the high rates. Of course the library will make them higher, for Mr. Carnegie will expect us to find a site and to maintain the ex- pected institution—if, indeed, be does not close his purse to us entirely after all the kind things we have I said of him ; but my point of view is that money spent on education, or on intellectual pleasures, is well- 'spent, and that, oven if it does increase the rates, the I game is worth the candle. If we want a library, we ought to be prepared to pay for it, unless some indeed, local Carnegie in a sudden acces sion of public spirit (and our rich men are strangely short of it), should see fit to give back to the town some portion of the wealth which he has won from its c,nitinuous toil. A spontaneous freewill offer- ing by a local citizen imbued with the desire to help his native place appears to me to stand upon a different footing than a benefaction "cadged" from an outsider, however laudable and generous his aims may be. And I do not like to think that any bumptious Yankee may at any.time, insult the Motherland by suggesting that we owe our intellectual opportunities to Yankee gold. The Warrington Library was the first rate-supported library in the country—a fact which, lam glad to announce, is about to be recorded on a table. I should like it to be the last to eke its fortunes out by asking alms.

div.head: TORTURED FOR TEN YEARS.
div.p: TORTURED FOR TEN YEARS.
Bile Beans Cure Chronic Indigestion
and Piles.

Mrs. Green, of 5, Green Man Lane, Hatton, near Feltham, recently told a remarkable story to a London ' Journalist :—" For 10 years I was a martyr to indiges- tion and flatulence," she said. " I was afraid to eat, for everything seemed to lie like a heavy weight on my chest. When I lay down the pain kept me awake, and my condition became almost unendurable. div.head: IMPROVEMENTS AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: IMPROVEMENTS AT FRODSHAM.

The Frodsham Parochial committee recommended (1) that the road channel at the entrance to the railway goods yard in Church street be improved (2) that the owners of the premises occupied by Mr. Andrew Hutchinson at the corner of Chapel lane and the main road be approached with a view to havin,, the sharp and dangerous corner of the wall rounded ofe; and (3) that the road leading from Sharp street to the waterworks pumping station be repaired. With regard to the first recommendation Mr. Diggle was instructed to get out an estimate as to what the work would cost. Mr. Stokes moved with regard to recommendation No. 2, that a signal be erected to warn drivers of the dangerous cross roads. Mr. Linaker: If people cannot take ordinary pre- cautions in the event of turning dangerous corners they deserve any accident with which they meet. It was decided to approve of the recommendation. Mr. Stokes gave notice that he would move that the County Council he approached with regard to the erection of a signal post. It was decided to take no steps with regard to the third proposal.

div.head: STORY OF THE SOUTH SEAS,
div.p: A STORY OF THE SOUTH SEAS,
DY HERBERT RUSSELL (Author of " The Zonphoreenan," c.)

Whenever we think of eternity. our fancy ,naturally takes flight into space. Distance seems 'inseparable from our ideas of futurity. Thus .Heaven is always overhead, let the hour Ile what .it will. The mystery of the blue void, being past human comprehension, tits in well with our shape- less fancies of that which also passes our mulct- standing. And yet who shall say that the im me- habit of disassociating thoughts of the ,future with materialistic conceptions is correct 't It is easy to trace the tuslioctive conneetitm be- tween the idea of what we dun't know, and what we can't see ; anti so. -Melt turn' their mental Vision upon the blankness of space when they seek lo locate those illusive dreams of Thuadise that through their brains. But bow do we know what lies, not over our leads, but under our feet ? Who can tell what is lirsid in the heart of this great world of outs, of --which we see but the outer crust ? Let me re- 'count an experience that befel me some years ago, the memory of which sets me musing in the fore- going strain.. . . . .

I was going out to Australia in a large full. rigged ship called the " Olyliurne." The reasons which induced .me to make the passage in It sail- ing vessel, instead if in one of the regular linen., are quite immaterial : suffice it if I say that. hav- ing plenty of leisure, I was simply following my inclination. We made a fine run down the long ,violet reaches of the Atlantic, rounded the Cape, and went bowling away " down our eroding ' style which set the skipper rubbing his loinalm, ,and kept hint on the broad grin of good humour. But when we had, struck the parallel of about E., our good luck deserted us. It was end- deuly dimpellad by one of the most violent temp- ests that ever poured across the foaming ocean. It came on front out of the south-west, then when it had riaen to the full volume of its fury, it backed into the south-east. For two whole daps it blew with ineredilde force : the barometer fell as low as 28.3, and yet never once did the s;irn of IL cloud appear in the clear blue of the sky. Upon that scene of hurtling waiters, with our ship help- lessly buffeted by the Andean billows, the situ shone brilliantly by day the stars winked with frosty clearness by night. The " Clyburne," hove-to under the merest shred of close-teefed canvas, made a brave light ,of it. But the straining caused by her giddy plunges and 14 tiggerifig upheavals upon the roaring cataracts which came in an endless Mow.. driven procession front out of the epray-shronded lemon, was more than any fabric put together by human bands could withstand. The gale broke early on the morning of the third day it dropped, with amazing suddenness, into a mere fauniug of air, leaving our ship wallowing amid -a confused jumble of swell, dismaated and sink- ing. . Happily two of our quarter-boats, together with the long boat, remained uninjured, other- wise our plight must have been a sorry one in- deed. When the carpenter had sounded the well for about the tenth time and reported the water in the hold gaining so rapidly, despite the cease- less clanging of the pumps, that it was impossible the vessel could continue long afloat, Captain 2ilarfell gave orders for the boats to be pro- visioned. Fortunately the sea subsided rapidly when the wind had gone, so that it was soon possible to lower the boats without any danger of their swamping alongside. Shipwreck, under the best conditions, is a most inconvenient experi- ence. But we were well in the truck of outward bound ships to Australia, although we after- wards discovered that the tempest had driven us nigh upon a hundred and thirty leagues into the mirth and west : with good boats and allundanee of provisions and water we had nothing to fear save front stress of weather, and barring this, 'night reasonably count upon being shortly picked up. When the vessel had settled so deep that every sluggish movement of her hull threatened to be the last plunge, we entered the boats and shoved off. I went, in the long boat, a tabby, roomy little craft : with flue were the Captain, -the third mate, and eight seamen. We had scarcely pulled away well clear of the " Clyburne," when she foundered. her going was not of that dramatic character with which sea- writers commonly in- vest their descriptions of sinking ships. She settled away from- view-upon at level -keel, vanish- ing so slowly as hardly. to leave an eddy upon the waters as they closed over the splintered etunips of her masts. The nearest land, lay the skipper's reckoning, was the Wand of Mauritius, for which he reselved to hear up. The three boats were put under can- vas : the wind being now no more than a soft summer breeze, and away we went, gliding quiet- ly over the long shouldering folds tif swell that brimmed to our gunwales. The two quarter boats drew rapidly ahead of us. They were of lighter build than the lubberly little craft I was seated in, and before sundown they had entirely vanished below the rim of the northern horizon. Throughout the night the wind held fair, and we made quiet but steady progress. It grew cloudy towards morning, and the breeze took a shriller note as it rolled out of the foot of our swelliog I cannot recall at what hour of the day it might have been, that one of the sailors who was standing up with hie tack' agaiust the mast, gaz- ing at the sea over the howm, siuldenly exclaimed, " Ain't that the ahadow of laud out there ?" I got upon my feet mud, following the direction in- dicated by his ,outstretched arm, thought I could make out a faint blue smudge against the misty gray of the sky that way : lint so vague that it melted when you looked straight at it, and was only dimly perceptible when you 'gazed a little on either hand of it.

" Laud !" exclaimed Captain Martell, letting go the tiller to shade his eyes • and stare. " Deuce a bit ! There's no land hereabouts nearer than some hundreds of miles—leastways according to the chart, or else I must be hideously mistaken in my reckoning." . " Yet land it is sir,". said one of the seamen, " and not so far off as it looks neither. There's a sort of mistiness in the air that makes it loom up big and far, like." He proved to be right. The outline of the mys- terious island shaped itself to our approach with a degree of rapidity which proved it to have been at no great distance when we first perceived it. A singular, ashen-lined hump of land it resolved itself into as we drew near, rising for about two 'hundred feet out of the ocean, and stretching for -It mile or so in length. The Captain steered straight for it, and when the sun was still three hours above the western horizon, we were with- in a mile of the island. '

" What a strange looking, inhospitable spot," said I. "A. volcanic roek," exclaimed Paxton, the third mate. " That's the reason it's not charted. Maybe its not been long born. One of those up- heavals from the bed of the ocean which sends a tidal waxe flowimr round the world. l've read of them, but never saw one before."

" Captain. " There's all the desolation of a fire-created island in the look of theplace. Just like a huge lump of pumice stone, isn't it ? Not a blade of grass nor a stalk of vegetation anywhere : nothing but ashes and lava. Well, we may as well go ashore, and have a look at the place anyhow, and stretch stir limbs for a bit."

He beaded the boat towards a little ledge that sloped in marble-smooth incline down to the wash uf the water. Her forefoot grated lightly, and She ran half her length high and dry. I took notice of a faint odour as of sulphur in the air, mid one of the men likewise remarked upon it. We stepped over the side one after another ; the stuff crunched under the tread, just like walking upon a cinder path, but accused a firm enough foothold.

" Lets heave the boat well up, my lads," said (be skipper. We mustn't lose her whilst we're Prowling about." We all laid hold of ber gunwale, and walked her up the slope well clear of the light wash of surf

We'll take a ramble round," said the Car- to me, stretching his arms and legs with ii air of a cramped man. " Pity we haven't :. Tjnion Jack to hoist, and take possession of the little kingdom in shipshape fashion." He and I sauntered straight up the central hil- lock, the others filing off in an aimless sort of Way. lii various directions. In truth there was Precious lit [he to be seen. Once or twice the stuff critelded under our tread in a yielding manner, ordl suggested that we bad better walk cau- " The place may he full of lava bub- bles," said 1, " and the crust might give way, and let us through at any moment." "['rue,' lie replied, and pausing he brought his heel down a ringing blow, as though to test Ihe solidity of the surface. Almost as he did so he tutored a i.hrirp exclamation, and tossed up his arias : a jagged gap yawned beneath Ida feet.
end he fell ihrougn. t WAR about a couple of yarda away from him at the time. Ho did not vanish entirely his head remaining above the level of the surface. " Are you hurt f" said I

" No," he unnwered. "My feet are on the ground luckily. This must be one of those lava bubbles of which you were speaking. Gad, though, it might have let me down far enough to break my neck I" I warily stdvanced to the brink of the orifice in which his shoulders were framed, designing in lend him a, hand to scramble out. But just as I wan in th 3 sot of extending my arms to him, the stuff yielded to my weight, and down I came. Being half prepared for this I was able to some extent to recover myself, and droripod on my feet; but the impnet of my figure against the skipper sent him sprawling backwards in a sitting pos- ture.

" Where are we F" says he rubbing his elbow with a laugh. I stooped my head to get a clear view beneath the surface. We had made a hole about five feet in diameter by fulling, and the daylight slanting in through this revealed a regular cavern, with dense, lustreless, black walls about ten feet apart vanishing into the gloom at either end. __
"A regular surl;terronean passage," said I. " Look et your bawls, skipper. You're squat- ted in a bed of soot !"
In fact the floor of the place was carpeted with the staff, like thick, black velvet. It was very worm, and the almoßphero Was strongly charged with that sulphuric odour I have already spoleen of.

" Below there !" called out the voice of the third mate above. " Are you all right it" His footstep sounded in a hollow crunching note overhead as be came to the edge cf the opening. " Yes, we're all right," I answered. ' Mind the stuff don't let you down too; " although even as I spoke I took notice of the feet that, owing to the arched roof of the subterranean passage, the crust was a good deal stouter where he stood and more likely to eupport him. " It feels firm enough," he replied, testing it by a quivering motion of his body. " What a queer place ! Shall I help you out of it P" The Captain, who continued to sit where I bad knocked him answered as he peered into the im- penetrable blackness at either end of the phort stretch of cavern that was visible to us : " a queer place, as you say, Mr. Paxton, and blessed if I don't think it's worth having a look at now we're down here. What do you say P" he added, addressing Me. "Why." said I, with a certain feeling of mis- giving as I strained my sight against the gloom, for the matter of that I am ready enough to go, but what are we to see by groping our way through such darkness as that P"

" Nothing. Paxton, just step down to the longboat, will you, and bring along (lip lamp that you'll find antler the stern sheets. Look whether tri iiiiii ed, and don't forget matches. Keep the men away from coming if you cam : we don't want a regular procession.'' " Ay, ay, skipper," quoth the mate, and away be went upon his errand. We squatted in the cavern, conversing about the singular discovery of this fire created island whilst we awaited his return. There was still a good two hours of day- light, and the Captain said he thought we should pass the night more comfortably ashore than penned up in an open boat. In about ten minutes Paxton returned, bearing the lantern, which he had already lighted. This lie passed down to me ;. it was a globe-shaped lamp, in a cage of brass wire, and gave a strong light. ' The Captain and 1 got upon our feet again, but were obliged to keep our shoulders bowed, so low roofed was the place. The third mate dropped through, and cowed beside us. " Let us go this way," said I, .flashing tha lantern around. " The cave looks to me to get higher a little distance along, and we shall be able to walk more comfortably. But we must keep our eyes sharply open for any bye passages. or else we may find ourselves in a kind of cata- comb, which will puzzle us ever to get out of again."

" Ay, and tread gingerly for fear of pitfalls," ridded the third mate. "We shan't be poisoned by foul air, I suppose F" " Sulphur is not poisonous," exclaimed Cap- tain Marfell, and with that we started, I lead- ing the way with the lamp. Our footsteps fell as noiseless as those of cat's upon the sooty carpet of the place. ,As I had predicted, the roof of the cavern soon became loftier : we had not gone more than about twenty yards when we were able to walk quite erect. The dead black walls absorbed the rays of light without throwing back any responsive gleam, and this made it difficult to guess the dimensions of the passage. But as it grew more lofty, so it certainly became wider ; the two men moved up, one on either hand of me, and so we advanced in line. I lowered the lamp to the ground at every other step, to make sure of our footing a yard ahead, !'and also swung it freely from side to side, that ,we might detect any openings in this singular cavern. But thus far all seemed as smooth and unbroken as a cor- ridor of black marble.

" We're going down a pretty sharp descent," said the Captain presently. "You may not only feel it in your legs, but see it by the way the place is enlarging as we go on. Why, it's as wide and high as the inside of a church now. Wonder where the deuce it leads to P" A little distance further on we turned a sharp bond, very cautiously making our way at this point, and staring keenly about us to make sure that there were no ramifications which might lead us astray. It was impossible not to feel the sense of awe and mystery weighing upon one in treading the silent galleries of the dense black cavern. That' my companions were equally sen- sible of this feeling, I could judge front the sub- dued tones in which they talked. " Gad 1" exclaimed the skipper, " I hope our lamp won't go out now." " Better turn bank at once if there's any likeli- hood of that," said Paxton, coming to a stop. " Not yet, anyhow. Even if we were left in utter darkness, we could make our way back all right by simply groping along the wall. Besides,. I for one, want to see where the place leads to." "It a uncommonly like the Valley of the Shadow," muttered the third mate, advancing with us again. " And almost as hot as the place beyond the Valley—that's to say at the wrong end of it," I added, mopping my brow. In truth, I was be- ginning to feel like Paxton : I knew he had had enough of it, and wattled to retrace his steps. But the skipper desiring to proceed, we neither of us liked to suggest retreat. It seemed to me as we continued our cautious advance that the at- mosphere of the cavern grew heavy with vapours. Although the lamp continued to burn with it bright flame, yet its powers of illumination became less and less. Like three shadows we stealthily made our way, always descending. It was al- most impossible to guess how far we had already come along the subterranean gallery, for out progress was PO PION', lint the passage of time af- forded no guide to the probable extent of it. We presently turned another corner. The sur- face upon which we were treading was less smooth now than it, had been, find I frequently kicked against little boulders, which I judged to be' lumps of lava. A faint moaning ;wise struck my ear, but PO feeble and indistinguishable that I' should have deemed it nothing more than a sing- ing in my head laud not the third mate also spoken of it. Capinin Martell said be reckoned it was the mound of the sea ; that we were probably approaching a lq.ot beneath the I.each of the island. and that the nohn we heard was nothing more than llie wash of 11. e surf :01.0ve.

" Stop !" exelaimed Paxton Fuildrnly, in i•oics which 1 'ream, •- -I•er frrror t. " I don't like this, %skipper. I for one am not iroing any furlle.w. If you two mean to go Of/ I'll start and grope my way back alone." The Captain made some answer, what it was I !soviet met end to reeall, for at this moment of coining lA, t. standstill, and gazing around me, a enoliah diswovery revealed itself. The %%ells land. roof of the place lied vanished ! The spikes of misty light slanting from the globular laolcrn disclosed the dend black ground whereon we stood, but nothing further. I held the lamp at srm's Imigth 311/191,0 my bead, swinginir it round to try and throw the light about as much as pos- sible. Ilut we seemed to be standing in a dense, impenetrable VOW. " Where are we?' I cried, noticing with dismay that any voice, which I pitched high under the iirst impulse of consternation, threw back no echo.

Captain I.larfe who was a 7111111 of extrnor- dinary coolness, Si mply gave vent to a low whistle of astonishment as he miln . his eyes, sodding in the lantern-light, round upon the pall-like curtain of gloom. 9 We're not lost anyhow," said he. " We've only got to follow our noses, and we're bound to strike one of the again, when it'll simply be ii mat ter of keeping abreat of it till it brings Us back to the place we started from." " Ay, but suppose we follow it in the wrong direction ?" said 1. - - - -

"Then we must turn round and work back ngain when we reckon we've gone far enough to sight daylight," he responded, still very coolly. " Are there no signs of our footprints P" sug- gested Paxton. " If we can see those it will be easy enough to follow the trail of them."

div.head: The-Examiner, Saturday, July 15, 1905.
div.p: The-Examiner, Saturday, July 15, 1905.

droppea upon my knees to scan the ground, ,holding the lamp within an inch or two of the surface. The substance which coated it looked to me to be a. species of lamp black. It was abso- lutely lustreless, and possessed a most extraor- dinary quality of absorbing the light. Not the faintest impression was visible upon it. Indeed, as I have said before, it was like staring at a sheet of black velvet for all that was to be seen.
"No footprints to be found here," said 1, rising to my feet again, with a sense of faintness beginning to come over me from the extreme heat.

"Never mind," said the skipper. "We know the way we came as near as possible. Let Us bead back in the same direction, and we're bound .to pick up our course before long." But we speedily found that we did not know the way we had come, seeing that we all three had a differt:nt idea as to the direction of it. However, we presently started again, advancing more cautiously than before, and straining our gage into the blackness at, every step in the hope of seeing the dull shadowy outline of the with. " Stand !" rang out the voice of the skipper suddenly, and the three of us came to a dead halt. The low, far•eff roaring noise which I have be- fore spoken of was taking a luuiiuui.r and deeper note, and there was a something in the character of it which persuaded me that it did not come from the sea. "

"We are going wrong !" exclaimed the skip- per. " I know it. You may tell it by that nosse growing louder itp‘tend of fainter." "That's so," said Paxton. Ws stood listening for a moment, and then the third mate added : "Where does the sound seem to you to come from P"

"Why I was just going to ask the very same question," said I. "If it was the surf, it ought to sound above our heads, for we must have des- cended considerably below the level of the sea. But as it is I am sure this peculiar moaning comes from the earth under our feet."

"So it does," said the Captain. " D'ye notice how much hotter the air has got in the last min- ute or two F" "I do that. Whew! I wish we were out of the smothering place." " So we shall be presently," went on Captain Marfell, still speaking quite coolly. " But we've come down here to see something, and since we're on the spot, we may as well look at it. I may be mistaken in my notion, of course, but I faney if we take just a few more steps we shall find the mystery of this cavern explained. Only for the love of God be careful how you freed : slide your foot along, and feel every inch oie.a with your toes before trusting your weight to i 0 Although I woulil willingly have retraced our way at once, as I am confident the third mate would also have done, yet I was conscious of a curious impulse to acquiesce in the skipper's suggesti n, and take just a few steps more. It was that morbid sense of an unknown peril, of mystery fraught with heaven knows what horror which fascinates men to steal close and peer be- fore recoiling. I lowered the light to within a band's breadth of the ground, lona in the crouch- ing position which this attitude gibliged me to adopt, I began to creep forward, the other two following just a trifle behind. My foot striking against a heavy stone, or lump of lava, I picked it up, and hurled it into the blackness ahead. It passed away bilently. I then felt about for, and soon -discovered, another stone. This I threw behind me in the direction along which we had just conic, and I plainly beard the sharp thud of it alighting on the carpet of lamp black.

"There is a precipice ahead of us," I said in a voice scarcely above a whisper, so soal•subduing was the feeling of awe and fear upon me. " As I expected when I told you to feel your way," murmured the skipper. "We are on the edge of the crater of this volcanic island. - The roaring we bear is from fire, not water, as the increasing beat will tell you. I want to reach the brink and look down."

Still under the spell of that morbid fascination which overcame my instinctive tendency to draw back, I crept. forward again, as cautiously as a timid man over yielding ice. I kept the light in advance of, me, to see the ground ahead as far as the rayless flame would reveal it, and this was therefore in my eyes all the while. But swinging the lantern sideways at the request of Paxton, and continuing to peer straight in fron of me, the faintest imaginable haze of ruddiness seemed to diffuse itself upon my vision. I know not how to describe the effect of that illusive sheen, whose far-awayness, so to express it, seemed only to accentuate the unutterable intensity of the black- ness. Indeed, it gave me the notion of the effect of a lurid reflection against the blankness of a blind man's eyes. A dozen more steps forward, and then there halted three startled, shrinking men upon the very brink of one of the most awful pits human gaze over beheld. The memory of that terrible spectacle recurs to me sometimes in a nightmare, in all the vividness of its incredible reality, and I marvel yet to think that my nerves could stand the brief but frightful strain of lingering within a few inches of the margin of such an abyss. Suppose the stuff had crumbled and given way beneath our weight, as it did on the surface of the island---! The horror of the thought makes me shudder as I write.

At our feet, through a shaft of blackness which sunk into the heart of the earth for heaven alone shall tell what mighty distance, there seethed, and waxed and waned, a lake of liquid lire. It had the hazy look of immeasurable remoteness, like the purple gusbings of one of those smoky sunsets you see in the tropics : but whether this effect was due to the gaseous vapours, or to the immense depth of that molten whirlpool, I cannot imagine. How we breathed the suffocating, sul- phuric fumes which rose oven-hot to our nostrils is another mystery I cannot lretend to explain At intervals long HUMS streaks of flame we'll& writhe upwards out of the crimson incandes- cence ; and once as we gazed there was a burst of sickly greenish-lined splendour, like a constel- lation of rockets, and for a minute afterwards the fiery lagoon seemed alive with tiny fleeting black shapes. The low, modulating roaring went on ceaselessly, and I laid not long been hearkening to it when I found my fancy creating out of the sound the wailing and moaning of myriad phan- toms down in those lurid depths. "God of mercy !" I ejaculated hoarsely. " Are we braking down into bell itself I" " What a sight !" muttered the Captain in tones which sounded strangely unreal. The third mate spoke not a word, and looking round at hint, I saw his figure shadow-like in the lantern light, beginning to sway in an °min- °UN manner. The terror of the thought of his suddenly pitching bead foremost into that frightful region of living fire broke the spell which was paralysing my nerves t keeping the ring of the lantern tightly in may grasp, I watehod an instant for a backward sway of his body. then grinpiir* his collar silliest with the lienzy of madness, 1 flung my full weight rear• wards, and the two of us went staggering several paces away from the brink of the pit. " Come I'. cried I to the Captain in a Voice like the croaking of a raven. " Let us retreat whilst , we can.'' " You are riglitliadi be, placing himself en the other side of Paxton's limp figure, mid link• ieg arms with him " Few men see as far into nature as it has heen given to us to do. - The sight will haunt me for a lifetime, for by my I.lher' 't believe the place was -full of fiendish spirits!" We began our backward march always tread- ing with the utmost caution. But the burning pit. had served as a sort of landmark to us, and we knew that by beading directly away from it, we Bhoula strike the gallery a gain through which we bad come. And thus it bliuttly proved. Never can I recall the like of the sense of joy and gratitude which swelled within me when, on turning a corner of the black 'cavern, we saw in front of us the blight star made by the daylight slanting through the orifice by which we had first broken into that weird subterranean region. A few minutes later we stood upon the surface of the Aland again : soot-begrimea, blinking, and . trembling and with the feelings of men who have not merely been face to face with death, but who were appalled by the awful fancy of having Peered into the realms of eternal damnation.
DRAW FOR THE THIRD ROUND.

The draw for the third ronnd of the works competi- tion took place on Nfonday evening. The following was the result : Corporation v. Longford, London and North-Western Railway Co. v. Rylands' No. 2 or Pletcher, Russell's; Pearson and Knowles No. 1 v. Whitecross No. 1. _ _

div.head: CHAMPION WRESTLER
div.p: A CHAMPION WRESTLER
Needs Zam-Buk After Meeting Haekenschmidt.

One of he champion wrestlers of England, Mr. J. H I Baldwin, of, 23, Wood-lane, Bothwell, Leeds, has been , indebted to Zarn-Buk over and over again. Not long ago, Hackenschmidt issued a challenge, offering £lO -to anyone who could withstand him for 10 minutes. Mr. Baldwin accepted the challenge and won it. "But," , says Mr. Baldwin, " I was terribly bruised and sore all over my body. Up to this event I bad been using for my injuries a kind of embrocation which I thought, and still think, a lot of. The recipe for it had been in our- family f over two generations. Now, however, I thought I would give Zam-Bok a trial. I rubbed the healing balm thoroughly into Or flesh—over every bruise and sore, till the stuff seemed to sink right in. I had two or three thorough applications like this,and was simply astonished at the result. Zam-Bnk stopped the pain and inflammation right away, and it was not long before the injuries were beautifully healed." Baldwin has also met Yukio Tani, the champion ; Japanese wrestler. In the match the Yorkshireman had the muscles of his shoulders and left arm seriously injured. "A medical man," says he," said it would be months before I should get better. Through using Zam- uk I hal the places soothed and healed in quite a ort time. I now use Zam-Buk constantly. It is the !finest healing balm I have met with in all my 20 years' experience." zam-Buk is also unequalled for skin troubles, such as pimple.. eczema, ulcers, bad legs, piles, diseased ankles, bad feet. chafing, heat spots, sunburn, rashes, freckles, sore backs, sore beads, barber's rash, ringworm, boils, 'abscesses, and also for poisoned or festering wounds. div.head: RUNCORN BOARD— OF GUARDIANS. The Boarding out of Workhouse
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD— OF GUARDIANS. The Boarding out of Workhouse
Children.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present—Messrs. A. R. Norman (presiding), C. Roylance, H. Eyes, J. Stokes, T. Baxter, H. M. Davies, J. If. Davies, J. Smith, T. Wright, T. Guest, S. Wood- ward, G. Pilling, J. Fryer, J. Stokes, L. Taylor, W. M. Morris, P. Collins, J. Douglas, J. W. Temperley, J. Rutter, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, R. Billington, C. E. Linaker, C. E. Linaker, jun., W. Weir, W. Turner, T. Antvris, and Admiral Jones-Parry and Messrs. J. T. Ashton (clerk), De Prez, Pearson, and Cook (relieving officers), and J. Cunnah (workhouse master).

•- THE BUCKLEY' HALL ORPHANAGE. THE QUESTION OF THE BOARDING OCT OF CHILDREN. The Clerk said he had received'a letter from the Brothers of Charity, Buckley Hall, Orphanage, acknowledging the receipt of the letter from the anardians stating that they could not see their way to increase the rate of maintenance of the boys now in the institution and chargeable to the Runcorn Union and adding that they could not keep the %children for less than 7s. per child per week and they requested that the children should be removed on or before the 15th inst. In reply Ihe had asked the Brothers to re-consider the matter. Since then he had received the account and had found that the Brothers had charged for 7 weeks at Gs. per week, and 6 weeks at 7s. per week. The Chairman: Six shillings a week is is. more than is charged in similar institutions such as Dr. Ba,rnados Home itc. In answer to Mr. Taylor the clerk explained that the Cost of a child in the Workhouse was from 4s. 6d. to ss. per week. The boy in the orphanage was almost 11 years of age and therefore almost ready to leave the institution. In consideration of that fact the Board might possibly decide to allow the boy in the orphanage as he was the only one who was chargeable. The Chairman : Personally I think, seeing this boy was accepted upon certain terms, it rather reflects upon the institution that they now threaten to turn him out because we won't pay an increased charge. Mr. Morris: I think the time has come when we should review the whole subject so far as Protestant as well as Roman Catholic children are concerned. It is quite likely there will be two morechildren whom we will be asked to send out, and I think we should decide whether we are to send them or not. _ . .

„. Mr. Collins moved and Mr. Pilling seconded that the extra Is. per week asked by the Brothers of Charity be paid. Mr. Woodward pointed out that the Board had sent the Roman Catholic children to homes and had paid more for their maintenance than they would have cost if they had been kept in the Workhouse. They could put the whole of the children in the Workhouse into institu- tions of a similar character for less money than they were now paying, or at any rate at no greater cost and in view of that he was distinctly opposed to making any advance in the payment for any child sent from the Union in the interest of any one section of the Christian Church. He moved that the increased pay- ment be not made.

Mr. Hallows seconded. Mr. C. E. Linaker : In the event at our not paying the increased cost the child will have to be taken back. Mr. Stokes said he would like to know whether the education given in other schools was similar to that, given in the Buckley Hall Orphanage ? The committee who visited the Orphanage were very much pleased with the manner in which the education was given. When any child showed an inclinatioa for any profession, the desire was developed. The Chairman : The education in other institutions is given on exactly the same lines. Mr. Morris thought equal treatment should be given to all children in the Workhouse, and thought the time had arrived when they should finally settle the matter The Chairman said he was very pleased with the senti meats which had been expressed. It is his intention to move at the next meeting that they should deal with all their children on the same lines as they dealt with the Roman Catholic children, Mr. Morris said he did not see how the Buckley Hall , authorities could charge the increased price as they had done, in face of the Clerk's request that they should I reconsider the matter. Mr. Collins : You cannot'expect to keep a child 14 years of age for the same sum for which you could keep a younger child. The Chairman : We have been sending children to the Orphanage for many years and they have remained until they were 14 years of age, but the question has not been raised before. The Clerk pointel out that if the boy was withdrawn the whole of the trade would be lost to him which he had been learning for the past 18 months. The ques- tion was as to whether they would injure the boy's chances by removing him at the present time. Mr. Hallows : Could not the boy be sent to another institution to finish his education? Mr. Morris : Under the circumstances we might let this particular case go. "qr. Woodward : I object on the ground of setting a precedent. This boy is almost LI years of age and has been one and a half years at a particular trade and would be able to .go as an apprentice to a shoemaker. I strongly object to the instituting of cf. precedent of this description. Upon the vote being taken it was decided not to pay the increased charge. -

FINANCIAL. Mr. Woodward reported payments of £914 Hs. 7d., including £OO 17s. 2d. vaccination expenses, and £428 2s. 6d. for the maintenance of lunatics. There was left a balance in hand of about £1,640. MR. RILEY'S SUPERANNUATION. The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board consenting to the proposals of the Guardians to add eight years to the actual period of service of Mr. T. Riley for the purpose of computing the amount of the superannuation allowance to be awarded to him in respect of his late services as relieving officer for the Frodsham district.

div.head: [Au. Marrs REszartn.] • A STORM AND ITS CONSEQUENCES,
div.p: [Au. Marrs REszartn.] • A STORM AND ITS CONSEQUENCES,
Fe C. SELOUS (Author ,f" Z•arel and .ddrenture in South East Africa," 4c.).

Towards the end of May of 1884, a full six weeks after the usual close of the wet season, the most extraordinary rain storm I have ever experienced swept over the desert to the west of Mutebeleland. I was at that time travelling slowly westwards by bullock waggon, following no track, but making my way across country under native guidance from one pool of water to another. One afternoon dense masses of black clouds gathered in the west, and presently spread over the whole sky. There was neither thunder nor lightning, but towards evening a strong wind sprang up, and soon afterwards a steady rain began to fall, at first light, but ever increasing in intensity, until &ton after dark it was coming down in such away that I thought it impossible that it could last long. But all through that night, and until midday the follow- ing day, the heavy rain never ceased to fall. During the afternoon, however, the sky again grew lighter, and the rain gradually ceased. By midnight the stars were shining from a cloud- less sky.
AFTER THE DELUGE.

Early the following morning I rode out to see the effect of this unprecedented downpour, and found the face of the country completely changed. On the sand ridges no difference was apparent. as the thirsty soil had easily absorbed all the rain that had fallen on it, but the inter- vening spaces where the Mopani trees flourish, and where the soil is a sort of light clay, had been transformed into broad shallow lakes from a few inches to two feet in depth. Riding across one of these flooded valleys, I came across a porcupine seated disconsolately on the stem of a fallen Mopaui tree—the first of these animals I hadever come across in the daytime. The sur- face floods soon soaked away on the level ground, but every hollow became a lake or pond which held water for a longer or shorter time accord- ing to its depth, and when traversing this same tract of country some five months later, I still found all the larger hollows fairly full, and was therefore able to travel at my leisure with ease and comfort through a country which in ordin- ary seasons would have been quite impassable by bullock waggon at that time of the year.
THE DESERT HEFRESHED,

Under these conditions I found this usually arid waste a very pleasant place to wander over. Game, though not very abundant, was still in sufficient numbers to enable me to keep my own people and the several families of Bushmen who had attached themselves to me in rude plenty. Owing to the favourable season all grazing and browsing aninials, including my own cattle, were in very good condition, and my larder seldom lacked the choicest portions of the giraffe, eland, gemsbuck and springbuck, four of the best ani- mals for the table, when in prime Condition, which South Africa, or any other part of the world, can produce. Blue wildebeests were more plentiful than all other species of game, and on the broad grassy plains which stretch westwards from Metse butluku—the bitter water—often congregated in herds of from one to two hun- dred individuals.

Here, too, large troops of zebras—Chapuian's variety of Burchell's Zebra—were often to be met with, as well as mall herds of the Cape hartebeest, now quite a scarce animal, as it has been either exterminated in most parts of its former range, or driven into the waterless deserts of South Western Africa.

div.head: SWARMS WITH GAME-
div.p: SWARMS WITH GAME-

In the dense thorn jungles which lay a little to the north of my route, a large herd of ele- phants spent the whole year, as I saw their tracks when travelling westwards from Math- beleland, and again on my return eastwards some five months later. These animals were, however, very wary, never drinking twice run- ning at one pool, and travelling immense dis- tances every night. I twice followed their spoor for a whole (boy, mid slept on it without coming up with them. But besides this large herd of cow and young bull elephants, there were four im- mense old bulls (judging from their tracks) which frequented the same jungles but lived by themselves apart from the herd. These old patriarchs I tried hard but unsuccessfully to find Lu the daytime, and I also watched for them at nights on several occasions at vleys at which they had been in the habit of drinking ; but I never had the luck to hit off the right pool of water on the right night. Once they drank at vley within a mile of the- one at which I was watc:hing, and I heard them at the water, but on this occasion I think they must have got my wind, as although I was early on their tracks and followed them all day Niith the best of Bushmen spoorers, I never got near them, and the next day rode home, shooting a fat giraffe cow on the way.
ELEPHANTS AND LIONS.

I may here remark that it is of little use, if you do not come up with elephants on the first day, to follow them any fur- ther, as if alarmed they travel very fast and far at nights, end on the morning of the second day will, in all probability be much fur- ther off than they were when you first took up their spoor. Of lions there were a few, but not very many in this part of the country. In one place, where the Bushmen had assured me there were none of these animals about, an old lioness had attacked and bitten one of my horses, though not very severely, and on another occa- sion I had found and taken up the fresh tracks of a lion and lioness, first in slndy ground where it was easy to follow, but later, in the bard, sunbaked soil in which the Mopani tree flour- ishes, and where I eventually lost it. At this time I had long been absent from the farthest outpost of civilisation, and had not seen a white man's face or spoken a word of English for more than six months. My waggon was then standing beneath some tall feathery-leaved thorn trees near a large vley of water, beyond which stretched a large open plain covered with a rather short growth of yellow grass for South Africa—as it was not more than about two feet in length. This open plain was skirted to the north by dense jungles of wait-a-bit thorns, and on its other three sides by open Mopani forest and scrub. My camp was on the northern side of the plain, quite close to the thorn jungles. I had plenty of books with me to read at nights, and hunting and collecting specimens of natural history tilled all my time by day. Ah those Were glorious times indeed.
