It is evident that Mr. BALFOUR'S neat little scheme of Redistribution pleases nobody. The Irish meniners ara not con- ciliated because he proposes to take away only •`1.2, seats from Ireland instead of 30. The Irish Unionists and their English sympathisers are indignant at this rnisplmed inKleratioa. As for the bulk of the Ministerial party, their real views find candid expression in the "Pall Mall Gazette." Not for the first thee that journal is outspoken in its condeinnation of Mr. BALFOUR'S policy. "The scheme has obvious imperfections, and imperfections of a kind of which its opponents will be able to take the most deadly advantage. It will only partially get rid of the Irish incubus, and it falters at the very point where the inequalities of the present system are most conspicuous and indefensible." What ars the inequalities of the present sysl ern ? They are surarnomed up in the admission of the "Pall Mall Gazette," that the new plan shows an unfortunate "tenderness towards the smaller con- stituencies." Mr. GERALD BA.LFOUR WOOld have ius believe that boroughs like Boston, Here- ford, Kidderminster, King's Lynn, Ponta- ' fraci, Salisbury, Shrewsbury, Stafford, Talll3tOnr Whitehaven, and Windsor are sanctified by " considerations connected with history and pre- ' scription, and the character of the communities represented." On this the "Pall Mall Gazette' grimly remarks that the character of such consti- tuencies is chiefly associated with the Corrupt Practices Act. "It is, of course, a mere coinci- dence that the exemption safeguards a cluster ef constituencies which are in the main faithful to one political party. But it is a coincidence upon which theother side can scarcely be expected to place the most charitable interpretation." In a worn the Government:are afraid to deal with the electoral anomalies in England. They are afraid to offena their suppirters who sit for small boroughs. They dare not provoke the wrath of Mr. Gibson Bowlee who is immortally connected by "history and pre- scription with King's Lynn" or Mr. Henniker, Heaton, who prophesied the end of the Govern- ment before the disfranchisement of his constitu- ency. By fixing the minimum of population for a con- stituency at 18,500, the Government propose t° sacrifice only four borough seats in England Boa Wales. Such a course, as the " Pall Mall Gazette" says, defeats the whole argument for reform. " To leave one single member borough with 127,000 inhabitants, and another with 19,000 would be to kindle the agitation for another Bill from the verY moment that the one proposed should pass into- law." It is a case, adds this unrelenting friend of the Government, in which those who are not pre- pared to complete their work would do much better to wash their hands of it entirely. They will ne wash their hands of it, however. They hope to I reconcile the critics on their own side by a flag- rant party manceavre. Of course, there is a shoW of increasing the electoral power of the great con- stituencies. London is to have five more seats. They could scarcely be denied. Besides, London is believed to be mainly Conservative in Paha° , mentary elections. But the manifest object of the scheme is to make as little change as possible in Great Britain, while materially weakening the Nationalist strength in Ireland. It is needle° to say that the Opposition will resist this picit on every ground. To call it reform is absurd - No champion of the Government is abl° to make out a decent case for it, and it is evident from the tone of the Ministerial journals that some of them at least have no inclins- tion to try. " Redistribution is a heavy task t° be attempted by a Government which is no longer . in its youthful strength. This is a very mild wed : of putting it. This Government has lost a Vai t deal more than its youthful strength. It has all moral authority. It is the most hopelessly dis; credited Government we have seen since 183f3. I hasipersisted in sticking to office in f national weariness and disgust, and 1 poses to remodel the constituencies its own interests—and incidentally, ' the dissolution for sixteen months I

div.p: The Conservative Labour Party speakers must have been disappointed with their reception at Wednesday evening's open-air meriting at Bridge- foot. The tariff campaign has fallen on evil days in Warrington as elsewhere, and the gloomy pictures of decaying industry quite Wel to produce the desired effect. It was evident that a fair proportion of the audience WAS Opposed to the views expounded, and there was -quite a fusillade of interruptions and chaff which seemed to grieve the stalwarts on the platform. One of the speakers, indeed, ventured to rebuke the workingmen for what he termed their lack of civility. The response came that the speakers " ought to tell the truth," and it is quite evident that Warrington workingmen are nor,i going to he gulled by the specious promises dangled before theru'by the preachers of Protection.
i
I

The news of the week, locally, is thst Admiral Nares, the acting Conservator of the Nferney, has refused his approval of the plans for widening Warrington Bridge by cantilevers. One cannot avoid the reflection that this is a sort of triumph for the obstructionists. With the Admiral on their side they will once again lift up their heads and sound a militant note.Presurnably the scheme will have to be re-consi.iered by the Council. We trust, bovvever, that they will not hastily abandon the cantilever project. Di was only carried in the face of strenuous and selfith opposition,and _ . . . .
the diffictilty with Admiral NAres sh;uld not be insurmountable. RatepAyers will call to mind the unpalatable f.ct that unless the widen- ing of the Bridge can he accomplished they

will soon be - salclled with the serlon-s -expense of a new structlre entirely. We believe that the great majnrity of the people in Warrnd- ton strongly prefer the cantilever scheme at abosa £3,000 to a new bridge it £20,000, end their wish :should be law in so far as the Corporation is con- cerned, while it is not to be lightly regarded even by Admiral Nam. We hope to see a strong line of action taken by the Corporation, sPeing that they are pledged to widening by ctntilevers.

Local Government Board inquiries are not the formal and perfunctory affairs that they used to . be in Warrington,when the Corporation borrowed money as it liked and satisfied the inspector in the simplest way without let or hindrance. Now- i- -days we heves vigilant " Non-Traders "and repre- sentatives of the Property Owners' Association attending the inquiry iii order that the itispector may be made CUgultimit of some of the more awkward fac a which are pert and parcel of the history of most public works.' The police buildings have this week been again on their trial before Colonel S!ecke, and it -cannot be said that they came out of the ordeal . unscathed. Councillor Pemberton, Mr. Goegh ' and Mr. England all had views to express and: , questions to ask which did not conduce to ' i harmony or the bettering of the Palace of Justice's ',. case. Originally the police buildings were tl cost £16,000, then the estimate swelled to £2o,ooo,and . ' 'finally, after a deputation had been to other towns and seen the sort of premises they must needs exeel for the honour and glory , of Warrington, the Stem of £25,0D0 was 1 : borrowed. Even that has not sufficed to ' ,i Day for; the huge" white elephant" in Wilson- fatten street,with its silent spacious corridors and ' numerous unoccupied rooms. Another 1:.1.500 isl required for extras, and oven yet the scheme is I , . nor, comoleted, though it was understood that the ~ buildings were finished when opened in 1902. The work has certainly dragged on in an unsetis-1 ' factory manner. and the expenditure involved . together with the nnwieldiness of the structure, !t. suggest that the Council passed the scheme with .i ..its eyes only half opened. However it (Miss he 'finally " finished " and if the additiomil £4,500 Will rneke an end of the job there will at bait be something to be thankful for. The Warrington Board of Guardians has not, :n 7 yet done with the accommodation question which , raised such heated discussion a short time ago. The Medical Officer again reports a general over- crowding of the hospital and Mr. Jenner Fast, the :;. inspector for the North Western district, is to meet the Board on the petition at en early date. .:- What the ultimate issue will he it is difficult to forecast, hut in deference to public opinion in view of the burdensome rates, the Board would !..,, be well edvised in net .attempting to force A more costly scheme than is absolutely necessary upon the ;.! Union. It is not long since Mr. Hickman sub- mitted propositions for meeting the difficulty ' ; without the erection of a new block by utilizing the I old infirmary and providing more workshops. It .:. was understood that plans of this scheme were to ..,..... be submitted to the Local Glvernment Board, but . so fat nothing has been heard from that authority. The merits of Mr. Hzekman's suggestions should , be fully discussed for they at any rate prove that •; ~ the opponents of lavish expenditure, so far from being inspired with that " selfish indifference to the sick and aged poor" which Mr. Jolley hinted . at, are prepared to make an honest attempt to solve the problem on economical lines. ... ---- ~ An end to Church d,ff srences is a consummation ~ Perhaps more than any other devoutedly to be wished. Dr. Horton, in paying, with the Free Church leaders, a courteous visit to the Baptist i 1 ' . World's Congress, now gathered in the metropolis, ' Was able to say that the welcome he extended ' Caine not only from Nonconformity, but—he was , informally commissioned to say—from the talalished Church as well. The fieliters in the Baptist, ranks—and passive resistance shows that - a few remain, though the abolition of war is a I i fundamental principle of the denomirettior. I --have accepted, with only a moment '3 hesitation, the challenge and the good . Wishes as well. This movement is onis of the forces of the new century. To most .1 7 important division of Theologians today is not into Catholics and Protestant into High Church and Evangelical, Conformity and Nouconfornyty, t critical arid uncritical. Tnere is a divisien which , cuts across all these. It ocmrs at the recognition and the non-recognition of the points of agreement ;• in all. Dean Stanley was a "universalist." Pro- lessor Drummond, too, said, with Hutton, that he . 'eonld sympathise with every Church but the Hard Church. There is a new unity in that spirit which h recognises the best contamed in every society and • method—Latin arid Greek Counties, scientific' thought, or Eastern philosophy. Comparative ~ theology is as important a study as theological ' . Polemics. , ' No subject in the history of man has had more .. fascination for him than the pursuit of the , oecret of life. Frankenstein's monster was a , •, Creation of which many had dreamt before the , , novelist put the dream into words and gave us the " Nameless Thing." Science, as it hiss developed, ~.. has cesselessly striven to find the source of what t, i know as life • and now, despite the dictum of ~ litualey and Tyr;doeil after long and weary experi- . menting that the search is nselese, we have yet another scientist who claims to have found the tnediurn by which activity may be put into the !lead,and the inanimate may become animate. It 38 cerions that just at this time Mr. S ephen Phillips should have taken the' Frankenstein . :theme to givens a play upon. Ayliner, in his latest work, makes a machine, pours into its month a licinid, and lo ! we have the Creature. Of Course, that is only the peg upon which to hang SOrn ....e poetry and declamation, many tine sentences, and a pathetic ending, such as it is Mr. Pnillips's 1 t ~rad eto produce. But all the saw, it shews how . curttle. forward we get, and how the old idea of e ; aaiting something that is hving,end is yet riot man till 1., runs in our minds. Mr. Phillips's play will !eta followed with the same interest that Mr. zittrirata experiments will he. The feeling that Iltli • • mates scientist, poet, and the man in the street it 3 much the same.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The popular query in Warrington just now is "Did he see you? "--a parody on "Have you seen the King?" Is there no local Carnegie who, in a laudable out- burst of public spirit, might solve the library exten- sion problem for us? Iloney made in the town might well be returned for so admirable a purpose.

Mr. W. L. Williams exp• ressed great astonishment on Wednesday that workingmen could patiently listen to the " harangues "of Mr. Joseph Howes and Mr. A. H. Crasfield but a voice from the crowd hastened to assure him that they will listen" to reason." That of course makes all the difference. * * * There is no truth in the rumour, persistently circu- lated during the past few days, that the procession of Roman Catholic school children, which was spoiled by the rain on Walking Day, is to be repeated on August Bank Holiday. Some of the scholars will, however, have another field day on that occasion. * * * " We want a change of Government ! " was the cry which interrupted Councillor Wilson's touching appeal at Bridge Foot on Wednesday evening for pro- tection for the British workman. That, indeed, is the feeling of the country as continually affirmed at the bye-elections and yet, in face of it all, Mr. Balfour and his followers cling to office with a remarkable tenacity. But the day of reckoning will come ! * * * Another speaker painted a glowing picture of German progress but when questioned was forced to admit that wages in Germany were not so high as in England. Thanks, of course, to the blessings of Pro- tection! Later in the evening there was also the gratifying admission that Germans came over to this country "to participate in the greater freedom and the higher standard of commodities." * * * It is a curious Net that while Warrington possesses some of the finest public baths in the North of England, there is no instructor in attendance to give lessons in the art of swimming. This is a serious deficiency which ought certainly to engage the attention of the authorities. The baths might serve a doubly useful purpose if all who patronized them were able to become proficient in the natatory art—if need be, by paying a reasonable fee. * * *

The thirteen farmers who were summoned at Dares- but on Tuesday for obstructing the highway with their potato market won their case, th ugh the magis- trates seemed to be of the opinion that the farmers had no right to stand where they did. For a while we suppose they will go on undisturbed, but the time is !Sound to come when the nuisance will be so real and troublesome that the farmers will be compelled to seek another market-place. * * * _ .

Our little crusade against the proposed Carnegie dole for Warrington receives support this month from an unexpected .though welcome quarter. Memnon in "The Dawn" for July sums up the case and decides against any begging appeal. " If we want a Library" says he "we should ba prepared to pay for it. . . , . . And Ido not like to think that any bumptious Yankee may, at any time, insult the Motherland by suggesting that we owe our intellectual opportunities to Yankee gold." Them's our sentiments too ! * * *

Great has been the joy of the "Heathens" this week for the train service to Victoria-scjuare is at last an accomplished fact. In their rejoicing the villagers have almost forgotten the threatened boycott, and -personal comfort has triumphed over conscientious scruples. There have been noble exceptions in the case of Parish Councillors, though even smae members of that august body have not been able to resist the temptation. The villagers generally have made the best of the matter by Raying the extra Id. and riding the full distance.

The great missionary of Empire has been filling the Albert Hall with grandiloquent assurances of a com- plete and final victory "—which, however, is not to come yet. A torch he says, has been lighted which cannot be extinguished. Wo agree. But who carries the torch ? All his efforts to extinguish Free Trade are manifestly futile. He calls it a superstition, and dismisses it to the Dark Ages of our political develop- ment. But to the great mass of people in this country it is still a fresh and inspiring flame quite hot enough o shrivel up Protectionist fallacies for an indefinite t eriod. * * *

" I have no hesitation in stating that our armed forces, as a body, are as absolutely unfitted and unprepared for war as they were in 1890-1900."— Thus Lord Roberts in the House of Lords on Monday. The telling indictment by the late :Commander-in- Chief ought to be posted in large letters all over the country. His words are a grave reflection on the Government which has controlled affairs since 1899, and on the war ministers, Messrs. Brodrick and Arnold Foster, who seem to have done nothing but evolve mutually-destructive schemes while the army has deteriorated both in numbers and efficiency.

*s* Mr. Chamberlain has lost a County Court action which was based on "preference." He was suing for damages to his brougham, and William Scott, the right hon. gentleman's coachman explained the accident. Asked if he thought he had a right to the road he replied: "Certainly. We take preference. Mr. Chamberlain is a public character, and. I was MN his business." "Oh," said counsel, "and you were surprised at meeting with retaliation." Preference ended at the Court, for Judge Woodfall decided against Mr. Chamberlain and dismissed the case. *s*

She had been reading the report of a county cricket match, and had come to the conclusion that it was a horribly barbarous game in which her husband delighted. " That Jessop is a perfect brute," she sobbed. " Whv ? How ? " asked the husband in amazement. ". Well," she went on, "it says he cut Hirst twice in the first over, and knocked Haigh all over the field. He drove Brown, jun., to the boundary and on Rhodes going on, hit him clean over the pavilion. Hirst came on again, and what do you think that Jessop did? He skied him and I suppose the poor dear man would have been killed only somebody with square legs ran up and caught him. That's why I say Jessop is a brute, and ought to be sup- pressed."

Mr. Balfour and the Government have broken faith with regard to the Unemployed Bill, which was: apparently only introduced for show purposes. Work- ' ing men, at any rate, will not be again lightly deceived after this by the magniloquent claims and promises of the Tory electioneer. This is merely a specimen—a good specimen, but only the latest arnong many—of the way in which the present Government has treated all the lust claims and aspirations of Labour. The Trade Dispute Bills were strangled with the same apologetic treachery. Labour never has got and never will get anything from aTo Government except by force; and force in this instance means turning It neck and crop out of the office which it has too long usurped. * * * Some of the listeners were not satisfied that the war office scandals should be so studiously ignored by the speakers at the. Conservative Labaur Party meeting and frequent unpleasant reminders of the dis- graceful revelations were forthcoming from the crowd. Then again, when Mr. W. J. Macartney pathetically asked " What is the reason for this unemployment ?" there was an immediate Iresponse of " The South African War," and the calm !assurance that the Conservatives were the friends of ; the working man was met by the query " What about I Chinese labour ?" Mr. Macartney's conviction that I the Government would pass the Unemployed Bill was warmly resented, for if workingmen had confidence lin the legislature to pass the measure,where would be the need for the demonstrations calling upon the Government to take these steps ? * * The potency of tl.e letters " V.R." or " ER." is illustrated by an amusing story related in the " Man- chester Guardian," which says : It may have been I noticed that "his Majesty's mail carts were expressly exemptad from the restrictions imposed upon wheeled 'traffic in the streets of Marchester on Thursday. This exemption is statutory, and, incidentally, gives a hard- worked body of men an exceptional opportunity a seeing Royal visitors at close quarters. When the ' King and Queen (then Prince and Princess of Wales) I came to Manchester in 1869 the descriptive writer of I that day , had just • made a note of "the splendid isolation of the Royal carriages as they rolled past ' the Infirmary when, much to his scandal and, indeed, to the astonishment of the spectators, a singu- larly shabby mail cart was driven rapidly up the otherwise clear route, was brought to within arm's length of the Prince's carriage, and then taken leisurely forward. It is said that the Prince of Wales was obviously annoyed at the incident, which was perhaps too dramatic a reminder of the virtue latent in the letters V.R.

div.head: Motor in Coll!son at Wlnwick.
div.p: Motor in Coll!son at Wlnwick.

As Lord and Lady Tollemache, who were en route Sunday in their motor-car from Teddington Hall to =fries, were passing though Winwick, his lordship, id endeavouring to avoid running over a dog, pulled to the other side of the road near Hermitage Green-lane, and ran into Miss Naylor, daughter of Mr. Peter Naylor, landlord of the Prince of Wales Hotel, Earlestown. Miss Naylor was cycling to Man- chester to spend a few days with friends, and was knocked off the machine with great force. Lord and Lady Tollemache at once rendered every assistance, procured the attendance of Dr. Harrison, of Newton- le-Willows, and had the injured lady removed home on the horse ambulance. NJ bones, fortunately, were broken, but Miss Naylor is suffering from severe bruises and shock,

ASH for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINER 9L WATRIM—Advt. Teachers' Association Picnic, The annual picnic in connection with the Warring- ton and District Teachers' Association took place on Saturday afternoon. Leaving Warrington in good time, the party travelled by conveyances through. High Legh, Hoo Green, Mere, and then arriving at Bucklow Hill, a halt was made for about an hour to. permit of Rostherne Church and Mere being visited. The drive was then continued to Bollington, where tea was served by Mr. and Mrs. Jefferson, of the Stamford Arms Hotel. After tea the village was visited as well as Dunham Park. The journey home was via Agden, Lymm and Thelwall. The weather was perfect, and though not so lase a number of teachers put in an appearance as might have'been expected, a most enjoy- able day was spent. Mr. A. H. Crosfield at Hariech. The links of the Royal St. David's Club at Harlech were the 'scene of an interesting match at golf on Saturday, when the Grand Duke Michael of Russia, partnered by Lord Maidstone. opposed Lord Winchilsea and Mc. A. H. Crosfield in a foursome. The party had driven over by motor-car from Bettws-y-Coed after lunching with Lord Winchilsea, and it included, in addition to the golfers, Prince Orbeliane, Countess Torbay, Baron and Baroness Stoeckel, and Miss Cros- field. The Grand Duke Michael has done mach to encourage golf at Cannes, where he is a regular winter visitor. Mr.- Crosfield, also, is well known on the Riviera; on more than one occasion he has brought over a strong team of British amateurs to play against the Cannes club. The match at Harlech was close and well contested; eventually Lord Winchilsea and Mr. Crosfield were successful by one up and -three to play.

On Wednesday evening an open-air meeting pro- moted by the Conservative Labour Party was held at Bridge Foot. Councillor W. J. Wilson presided over a good attendance, and devoted his speech to ; an advocacy of tariff raform. He hoped, he said, they would live.to see the day when England would be supreme once more in her exports of manufactured goods and that the production of Germany and America would only be • second-rate to England. Councillor Wilson declared that while works in England were ; running short time, the workmen of America were ' employed " from sunrise to sunset " (Voice from the .crowd : " Nonsense ") Further remarks by the Chairman were greeted with the cry : "We want a &long° of Government"—The principal speakers were : Mr. W. J. Macartney, Hr. J. Raymond, and Mr. Robert Orrell, but their remarks were continually interrupted' by the crowd—Mr. W. L. Williams proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers and said there ap- peared to have • been an organized attempt to interrupt the meeting (Cries of " No.") If that that was to be the Policy of the Radical party during ! the campaign, two could play at the game (A 'voice : " We have got sick of listening.")—Mr. J. J. Hinds , seconded and said that after forty-dx years residence in Warrington he was sorry he had, had to come into contact with workingmen ayho were devoid of civility. In acknowledging the vote of thanks Mr. Macartney said two represent dive Conservatives (mid be pre- pared to discuss questions of social reform and as to which party had done the most in the interest of the workers with two representative Liberals (Workingmen for preference) who were citizens of Warrington. tie personally would be prepares to debit° th 3 questioa ! with the Independent Labour rarty in that party's own

div.head: Attempted Suicide.
div.p: Attempted Suicide.

At Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, Patrick M`Donough, labourer, lodging at 39, Rose and Crown- street, was brought up on remand, charged with attempting to commit suicide by cutting his throat with a razor a week before. Superintendent Monaghan stated that prisoner had promised not to attempt to take his life again, and on that understand- ing he would offer no other evidence. In discharging prisoner the chairman said he hoped it would be a warning to him.

PUBLIC BEREFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS Di LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Sanday School Teachers' Picnic. The annual picnic in connection with St. Paul's Church and All Saints' Sunday Schools took place on Monday, when Farndon was visited. The party left by train for Chester at 1.15 p.m, in special reserved carriages, and on arrival at the ancient city waggon- ettes were in waiting to drive to Farndon the drive being a most enjoyable one. A substantial tea was provide iby Mr. McCreadie, of the Raven Hotel. and the remainder of the time vela occupied in walking through the lovely district. Some visited the inter- esting churches of Holt and Farndon. Home was reached about 9.30 p.m., the party having thoroughly enjoyed themselvee. They. were acc impanieri by the Vicar and Mrs. Btacecamp, the Rev. it. H. Bowen and Mrs. Bowen, and several members of the congrega- tion.

"PREMTETL" CYCLES at 7 guineas startling value.— J. S. GA.RLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge St., Warrington.— Advt. Warrington P.S A. An open meeting of the above society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Sunday when a large number of members and friends were present. Mr. E. W. Jones (president) occupied the chair. The Legh-street Methodist choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Spruch, ably rendered the vocal items "Call to remembrance " and "Hark, hark, my soul," the solos being taken by the Misses E. Woodland, L, Snelling, A. Bridge, and Mr. C,ortin. The accom- panist was Mr. B. Wadsworth. The Rev. F. Vaughan delivered an address, in which he referred to the rough judgment men were prone to pass on their fellow men. Every Christian body came in f w juagment ; in fact, everybody was judged by the world at large, but he thought that in this Christian country of ours we might at least learn what the motives of men were before we were too harsh in criticizing. ASH for CITNELNIGHAM'S VILNERLL WLTERS.—Advt. Local Oddfellowship. The half-yearly meeting of the Warrington district of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity) was held at the Traveller's Rest Lodge, Stockton Heath on Saturday, District Grand Master 1. Taylor presided and was supported by D.D.G.M.T.P. Bradshaw, D. Treasurer, T. Wadsworth, and corres- ponding secretary P.P.G. Mr. Frank Webster.—The statement of accounts was Presented and approved. The sum of £5 Was voted as a grant to the Warrington District Nursing Association.—P.G. George F. Free- man was elected* auditor for the ensuing year.—P.G. William Holbrook and P.G. George F. Freeman pre- sented a report on their visit to the A.M.C. held at Plymouth during Whit week. The subjects dealt with included the Workmen's 'Compensation Act, the secession o branches, and the initiation of juveniles into the Order over the age of twelve months. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting. IL M. ASHTON'S Lire Tostc aids Digestion.— (Advt.) Trades Council and Women's Franchise. -

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council which was held oo Tuesday a letter was read from the Womens' Social and Political Union, asking the Council to receive a deputation to address them on the Womens' Enfranchisement Bill. Mr. Grealey moved that the letter lie on the table. For a long time he said the Council had been drifting away for the purpose of which it was originally intended. Trade was almost lost sight of and they were drifting into politics.—Mr. Plumb explained that the whole of their work was political but not party political.—Mr. Grealey strongly contended that the Womens' Social and Political Union was a political 'Union, and that their representative should not be allowed to address the Trades Council. The question of a franchise for women was a political one, and should not be entertained by the Trades Council. —lt was, however, decided to invite a speaker to address a meeting of the Council.—Mr. Grealey asked whether the Secretary had made enquiries as to the painting of the tramcars.—Councillor Stott said he had not suffi- cient information to enable him to present a report on the subject. He hoped, however, to be able to report to the next meeting of the Council, PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER tr•RE CLOCIt FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. 1.0.G.T. _ The monthly session of the above was held on Saturday in the St. Paul's Girl's Institute, Al forde- street, Widnes. The session was opened at 3.30 p.m. There was a goad gathering of members, over fifty being present and representing all the lodges in the convention area. Interesting reports were given of the various lodges showing their progress since the last meeting. Notice was also given that a new lodge was to be opened at Downhell. Green on July 25th next. This was received with applause. The session was closed just before six o'clock, and an excellent tea was provided by the members of the Widnes Con- solation Lodge to which ample justice was done. In the evening a public meeting was held in conjunction with the mission which meets in the St. Paul's Girl's Institute. Bro. G. Clarke of EarleStown occupied the chair and addresses were delivered by Bro. J. Parr , (" Happy Jack ") the converted collier of Leigh, Bro. F. Merlin of Warrington and Bro.J.Pugh of Oswestry. These were interspersed with hymns out of the Church Army hymn book, and a good meeting was brought to a close at nine o'clock.

Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Co., Ltd. In their report to the shareholders the directors of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Co., Limited et tte that the gross -profit for the half year ending 30th June last, after providing fir all bad and doubtful debts. is 1228,947 2s. 2d. to which has to be added the anima brought forward from 315 t Decem- ber last, viz.: £35,529 14s. 11d., making a total of £264,476 17s. Id. 'From this sum the following deductions have to be made —Total expenses at the Head Office, London Office, and Branches, including salaries, stationery. taxes, &c., £81,935 18s. 2d.; half. year's provision for income tax. £5,000 ; leaving a .net profit 0f.F.,177,510 18s. 11d. The directors recom- mend the declaration of a dividend of 21s. per share, which will take £131,250, leaving a b dance of £46,290 18s. lid. Of this it is proposed to carry to the reserve fund £lO,OOO and to next ace mart:31,290 18s. 11d. The reserve fund with the absive addition will then amount to £1,815,000. During the past half-year offices have been opened at St. Annes-on-the- Sea, at Tean as a sub-office to Cheadle (Staffs.), and at Marple Bridge as a sub-office to MArple. Arrange- ments are being made for opening shortly at Reaviloy (Stockport), and at Hollins Grove, near Datwen.

On Saturday the 174th District quarterly meeting in connection with the Ancient Order of Foresters was held at the Mason's Arms, Mill-street. Bro. William Hipkiss,. District Chief Ranger, pi esided and was supported by Bros. R. Thorn/ey, P.D.C.R., G-eorge Maybury, P.D.C.R., and P.C.R. Wilding. It was reported that the membership of the district was 1,092 ordinary members, 73 widows; 18 new members were added to the register. Throe., deaths had occurred during the quarter. It had been _decided that as the North-Western Federation of ForeSters which com- prise Courts and Districts of ;:Lancashire, Cheshire, Derbyshire and Flintshire had agreed to h dri its next meeting in Warrington and a strong committee was formed to make all arrangements for the hold- ing of the same on the '23rd of September. Houghton on his return from Crewe on June 17th. His triumphal entry through our village on June 17th, as Grand Master of the Order of Druids, will be long remembered by those who witnessed it. Co-operative Society Picnic. 1 The employes of the Warrington Co-operative Society held theit annual picnic on Tuesday when a visit was paid to Llandudno. About 100 left Bank Quay station lat 8.20, the Welsh watering place being reacho some I two hours later. No official programme had been arranged and the party were left to their own devices. Generally speaking, the weather was fine, though there was a heavy shower in the afterno in, and the trippers greatly enjoyed the out. Warrington was reached at ten o'clock. Serious Accident to a Warrington Lady. Mrs. Clarke, wife of Mr. E. W. Clarke, Sinkey, met with a serious accident whilst cycling on Wednesday. She was proceeding along Parker-street in the direc- tion of Bank Quay Station when she collided with a cab, which, it is stated, was on the wrong side of the road. Fortunately the horse swerved as Mrs. Clarke fell but the wheels of the vehicle passed over her back. _ _

She was immediately conveyed to the Infirmary, where it was found that she was suffering from severe shock. Her right hand was much lacerated awl her left leg severely injured, though fortunately no bones were broken. Her injuries were promptly treated, and her many friends will be glad to learn that she is progress- ing favourably. New Wesleyan Ministers for Warrington. The Stationing Committee of the Wesleyan Confer- ence has prepared the " first draft" of ministerial appointments, and a copy of the document has been Sent to every minister and circuit steward in the con- nection. The appointments are subject to further revision when the Conference meets. The two new ministers drafted to the Warrington circuit are the Rev. Sidney Pitt and the Rev. William Mellor. The first-named is chairman of the Isle of Man District where he has workeA for the ppt three years. while Mr. Mellor has been stationed at Woolton for four : years. The Rev Sydney Pitt will succeed the Rey. G. H. Carnson (superintendent of the circuit) who at the beginning of September goes to Wigan, and the Rev. William Mellor will take the place of the Rev R. Wilkins Rees whose new station is Fleetwood.. The Per. John Gunnell, supernumerary minister, Periketh, has now ceased his official connection with the Circuit and the conference has decided to appoint a young minister who will have charge of the Penketh district. The minister has not yet been selected. H. 14. ASHTON'S Live ToNrc cares Sleeplessness. —(Advt.) Christian Endeavour Ramble. The annual "Ramble and echo meeting" of the i Warrington and Distric,t Union of Christian Endeavour Societies was held on Saturday at Hill Cliffe. At three o'clock about 50 met for a ramble, and, under the • guidance of the President of the Union (the Rev. J. S. Hughes), various places were visited and a delightful walk was experienced. A return was made for tea in thc schoolroom where others had also assembled. The tea was under the directlon of Mrs. Hughes, Mrs. Wheeler, Misses Mather, Jones, Dodd and England. After tea there was an echo meeting in the Chapel, presided over by the Rev. J. Hughes. The Chairman stated that the purpose of an echo meeting was to hear reports of those who had at- endsd the.grast convention of endeavourers at Birming- ham. The Rev. H. Wall offered prayer, and interest- ing addresses were given by Miss 'Welford (Lymin). Misses Mason and Liddle (Warrington), and Mr. Mason, A pleasant surprise was also givens by the presence of the eminent Welsh singer, Ur. Enelyn Davies, who charmed his hearers with " Channels only." , Order of Druids, The quarterly district meeting of the Druids Friendly Society (Warrington Equalized District Branch), was held on Thursday at the Blue Lion Hotel, Gratid- Master William•Hankey presiditig over a full attend- lance of delegates comprising the 13 Lodges. The. Secretary, Bro. E. Allen reported a new membership of 16 males and 7 wives for the quarter and a total net increase of fends of £lO5 Si. which was considered highly satisfactory. The funds are well invested and the Order as _a whole is in a very healthy condition. Progress has been made and it WAS the !unanimous wish of the delegates that it shotdd be maintained and continued. The Delegates report of the A.M.D. proceedings at Crewe was given by P.G.D.M. Bro. 'Win. Bibby. It was especially men- tioned that the rule relating to Accident. Compensa- tion (which empowers the Board of Minagement to grant any sum not exceeding £lOO to any member who meets with an accident) was rescinded. It was felt I by. the original Advocate of this fund that it had now lost its usefulness throu4ll ths operation of the Employers' Liability Act. A hearty and Unanimous vote of thanks was given to Bro. Bibby for his able report and it was decided to have comes printed and circu- lated amongst the members. Bro. Robert Perdue was unanimously elected district treasurer and Bro. George Rigby was re-elected district auditor. A large amount of business was got through and the meeting was'the most successful and harmouions that had taken place I for some considerable tune past.

div.head: ! WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: ! WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
Admiral Sir G. Hares ejects the
Cantilever Scheme.

We are informed that Admiral Sir George Nares, Acting Conservator of the Mersey, has refused his approval of the plans of the proposed widening of Warrington Bridge by means of cantilevers. The reason stated for the refusal is that the alteratioa would interfere with the navigation of the river. It will be remembered that at several meetings the Town Council d.scussed the merits of two schemes suggested for coping with the congestion of traffic on the bridge—the erection of a new bridge, and the widening of the existing structure by cantilevers at each side. The cost of the resmctive schemes is roughly estimated at ;£17,000 far a new bridge and i.:3,000 for cantilevers. After full consideration the Council decided in favour of the latter praposil, but before the work could be proceeded with the approval of Admiral Sir George Name, as representing the navigation authorities hid to bs ob-tined. His decision means that the whole question will now have to be re:!ousiderel by the CJuncil.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

A friendly match with Bollington was Warrington's fixture for Saturday, but tee heat WAS so oppressive as to make cricket exceedingly hard work. Nevertheless there was some excellent batting, partic ilarly on the Warrington side, but neither eleven could claim the advantage, as the match resulted in a draw. Warrington went to the wicket first and arnass,d the substantial total of 262 for the loss of font wickets. Bollington had an horir and a half in which to save the match and thanks to V. Hope and T. Clay they performed the task with ease. only one wicket having fallen at a cost of 67 runs when the game closed.

On the Warrington side W. H. Podmore carried off the batting honours. His was in-leaf a brilliant innings and he was sorne chat unfortunate in not attaining the century, his display Wini. resp msible for 93 runs. This is the largest score that Podrnore has made for the club, and his chief hits included fifteen fours. P. B. Hawtin and E. A. Connor were both in splendid form, and com- piled 41 and 40 respectively. A characLeristically vigorous innings by J. W. Bibby realized 37 not out, while Mason knocked up 20.

Sankey Wire mmi 2ui eleven are playing well at present and on Saturday defeated Cronton Ist by the large margin of over 10) runs. For the Wire Mills, R. Walsh and T. ViThittleld batted in fine form for their respective totals of 53 and 34 not out. Cronton failed entirely in their task of getting Past the total of 128 scored by the Wire Mills—indeed they only managed to score 27 all told. For this some good bowling by S.Partridge was mainly responsible. Partridge's analysis read 8 runs 6 wickets. The fielding of the home team was pretty good which is not always the case in junior cricket, by an means. It may be mentioned that Wire Mills nlso defeated Crouton at Crouton snmA weeks back. To-day the Wire Mills meet Grappenhall 2nd, at Grappenhall. -- 1 Warrington second were victorious over Bollington 2nd, the margin being 23. R. Pierpoint was the top .scorer with 31 to his credit. Bainbridge captured two Iwickets for no runs.

-- -- There was an excitinglmatch between St. James' and Latchford Baptists 2nd, the former having, the good for- tune to win by a single rim. There was no particularly good scoring on either side, S'lerratt's innings for 14 being the best performance.
Warrington Mersey triumphed over St. Mary's by 63, Rutter batting splendidly for 19.

The principal feature of the match between Monks Hall and Co., and Cheshire Lines 2nd was the low scor- ing on both sides, seven being the highest individual total and nine players failing to open their accounts. The tesms were so evenly matched that a tie resulted.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The Corporation green in Victoria Park has evidently supplied a long-felt want in the district, as judged from the extent to which it is used tiy trundlers resi- dent in that end of the town. A steady average issue of some 400 tickets is being maintained, and in the evening every available inch of space on the green is utilised —in fact a much larger green would hardly meet the demand. Some doubt seems to exist a, to the rules with regard to the hiring of the woods. Every trundler hiring bowls is entitled to the use of the green for an hour, with the option to continue for another hour at the expiration of that period. At the end of the two hours if there is any de:nand for tlas woods he is bound to give them up and make way for other players. Persins nsiag their own bowls can use the green for as long a period as they desire, provided, of course, they make the neces- sary payments.

The rules for the Warrington Works Competition are by no means perfect. Last season an unexpected situation arose which prevented one of the teams from taking part though the breach of the rules was the result of unforseen circumstances over which the players had no control. This year another difficulty has been experienced which necessitates the re-playing of a match. Rile three provides that bowlers shall be eligible if they have been employed by the firm they represent for four weeks prior to any particular fixture. Rule four how- ever states that in the event of any woiks running two or more teams the players in each team shall be registered before the opening of the season. The reason for this is obvious and is to prevent any player from ' playing for more than one team, but why should the players be registered ? The object could easily be achieved without the necessity of such a proceeding.

There is no need to take a hypothetical case to show the injustice of the present rule as a striking instance has been afforded. Georae Shaw. a bowler of undoubted skill, entered the service of Atessrs. Rylands Bros.. though too late to be registered as a representative of either of the teams connected with the works. He was qualified to play under the first rule and did assist liylands No. 2 team on Saturday in their match with Fletcher's. Prior to the commencemant of the game Fletcher's entered a protest, but the fixture was completed, and resulted in the discornforture of Fletchers• men by the narrow margin of four points. A technical breach of the rules, had, however. undoubtedly been committed, and the appeal by Fletchees has 'resulted in the match having to be re-played.

Nothing could be more finjust but the committee had no option than arrive at that decision and the hardship lies in the rules, Rylands won a hard fought—game a victory which was not claimed until the last men were off the green—and deserved to qualify for the third rounP, but perhaps they will accomplish their object to- day. Tdo not wish it to be inferred that I accuse Fletcher's of unsportmanlike conduct. On the contrary they were perfectly justified in their action. Their protest was entered before the match commenced and had they won the matter would ri tin have had to go before the committee.
The other match which was decided was not produc- tive of much excitemmt as the ChoAire Lines Com-
mittee team stood no chance against last year's champions and were defeated by 30 points.

The draw for the third round has resulted as follows : —Corporation v. Longford; London and North Western v: Rylands (No 2) or Pletchers ; Rylands (No 1) v. Pearson and Knowles (No I) ; Whitecress a bye. To- days matches are Itylands (No 2) v. Pletchers (second round) ; and Corporation v. Longford (3rd round.

Tile Cemetery Hotel I players are to-day expecting to avenge their defeat at home by the Bull's Head club by whom they will be entertained. Their success is doubt- ful but they certainly will give the prospective champions a good game. Fearnhead visit the Horse and Jockey green, and will in all probability drop a couple of points.

A Tosague team should on Thursday have journeyed to Runcorn to meet the representatives of the Runcorn and District League. On account however of the Royal visit VI Manchester their visit was postponed for a fortnight.
Altrincham Conservatives on Saturdiy visited War- rington when they met the team connected with the senior club and were most thoroughly beaten, winning but three games out of the 22 played.

'The third handicap promitted by the Prince of Wales Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Man- chester Unity) will be held at the Farmer's Arras, Fearnhead, on Stturdav, the 22nd inst., when the Crostleld cup and medal and other prizes will be com- peted for. There is every prospect of a splendid entry.

Councillor W. Brough entertained the journalists of Warrington at his residence at Fearnhead on Wednesday afternoon. The primary object of the visit wls to decide a bowling main on the excellent green which Councillor Brough has ;had laid in his garden, and the affair proved most enjoyable. Some of the pressmen can claim to be expert trundlers, while others made their first practical acquaintance with the game, but nevertheless there was a series of interesting contests. Toe final produced a splendid game between Mr. 11. Isherwood and Mr. A. H. IValker, the first-named winning by a good margin. The company sat down to an excel- lent tea, and luring the evening visited the well-kept grounds of Mr. Thomas Birtles, who took photographs of the group. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Councillor and Mrs. Brough for their hospitality and a similar compliment was paid to Mr. Dirties.

The final for the Allison Cap, open to members of the Cemetery Hotel Club, produced an exlitin,, struggle between T. Ellison and T. Bolton but the Gilt-named triumphed by a very close margin. This being the third time Ellison has won the cup it now becomes his abso- lute property. The other prize-whiners were : P. Bolton (2), R. Young (3), T. Cooper (4), W. Hill (5), J. Wood (G), and G. Ball (7).

Cycling. There was a record turn-out of the members of the Warrington Cycling Club on Saturday, when the annual run was held to noeston Towers, the residence of the president Mr. J. Naylor. The weather was beautifnlly fine and the day's proceedings, which are fully reported in another column, were very successful,

The inclement weather on Tuesday evening militated against open-air enjoyment and only six members of the Warrington Club turned out for the ran to Boiling- ton. Arrived at their dastinttion the evening was spent at the Stamford Arms and the party spant a very enjoyable time.

Local Athletes' Successes. Warrington's athletes were again among the prizes last week-end, some exceptionally creditable successo- being achieved. In the first plane, hearty congratula tions must be accorded to C. Berry, the well-known Warrington Cyclist, neon winning the mile N.C.U. (Manchester Centre) Championship at the Nlanchester Wheeler's sports. It seems but a short time since this young rider came into prominence in the racing world, and to have won the championship is no mean honour. The race produced a stiff struggle between Berry, W.H. Crump, Salford, andl'. R.Gibson, Manchester Wheelers, but Berry showed splendid finishing powers, and just got home by half a wheel, in 2aain. 40 2-ssecs.

"Sprinter" in the "Athletic News" thus speaks of Berry's success :—Hail Berry! One likes a chap with a merry red face; one that laughs "no" to you when you persist be should sit for his photo, and yet, like the Poet Byron's maid, whispering he would ne'er consent, consented. Charles Berry is a ruddy-faced son of the soil, with a turn of speed appreciated by the handi- cappers, for he is estimated as speedy as Scotland's representative, J. Haig, jun. If that be so. the Manchester Centre has some rare millers, for in the local championship over 1,760 yards we had a series of heats which would be difficult to beat for closeness. W. H. Cramp beat J. A. Dobson, the girl-boy from Bury, in 2min. 21 1-ssecs. ; Harold Dixon vanquished George Jones in 2rnin. 16 2-ssec. ; E. Ban'u; qnelched his opponents in 2min. 37secs.; and T. R. Gibson stayed just the trifle longer than H. English land P. Ward, in 2min. 41 4-ssecs.—after a desperate set- tn. The standard was 2rain. 20sec., so Dixon and George Jones alone earned those medals. In the final Crump was always nicely placed, but Dixon was just as badly circumstanced, and after Cramp had looked like winning as they wheeled into the straight, Berry got up and beat Crump a wheel in 2ruin. 40 3-ssec., Gibson Iscrambling into third position. But, hail Berry ! He is a solid little fellow—one of the useful sft. 71n. brigade, little and good. Crum's form, however, would suggest that he had reserved himself for the medal. He has never ridden so brilliantly this season. With such raw material as Berry, Cramp, and Dixon—could they be transferred to Scotland—the S.C.U. would be looking forward to the next B.E.,Championships. ' Warrington competitors figured succ6ssfnl at the Widnes Amateur Athletic Club's sports on Friday and Slturday. R. Dimbobbin, of Latchford, was a good third in the 120 yards fiat race (district), the time being 11 4-5 secs. H. Mounfleld. Warrington, obtained third place in the two miles bicycle handicap (districts). In the 120 yards (open) flat race, two prizes went to War- ringtonians. J. Corradine running in first with J. Moran second. The event of Saturday was the two miles scratch Ince A. Shrnbb, the famous runner, carrying off first honours by 160 yards. J. Roberts, of Sefton, was second, while O. J. Straw,of Warrington, came ia third. The second prize in the two miles bicycle race (open) was captured by J. Houghton, of Stockton Heath. At the Doncaster Rovers sports J. Riley, of Warring- toi% was first in the mile flat race.

THE ROYAL VISIT TO MANCHESTER. Lord Mayor Knighted A NEW DOCK -OPENED.

The visit of the King and Queen to Manchester on Thursday was favoured by splendid weather and the city looked very gay in its holiday garb. On arrival at Victoria Station from Knowsley,where their Majesties had been the guests of the Earl of Derby the King wore the undress uniform of a Field Marshal, and the Queen was in a gown of light pink. At the Town Hall, where their Majesties at once drove, a con- spicuous group was that of the officers from the French cruiser Duguay Trouin, just now lying in the Mersey. The King bestowed on them a special mark of reoogni- tion.

_ A congratulatory address from the Corporation was handed to their Majesties on a solid gold salver ; and the King made the folilowing reply: I thank you heartiv on behalf of the Queen and myself for the loyal and dutiful address you have presented to me, and for the good wishes for our welfare which you express therein. We tvell remember our previous visit to this great city, and it is a sincere pleasure to us to have an opportunity of meeting once again the inhabi- tants o Manchester, and to be present at the inauguration of a new dock, which will, I feel sure, by affording additional accommodation for the traffic on the canal, give increased commercial facilities to a wide area of manufacturing districts around this city. It has given us the greatest gratification to witness the cordial demonstrations of loyalty and attachment to our persons which we have met with during our visit. MAKING A NEW KNIGHT. Next followed a picturesque incident., evidently unex- pected by the bulk of those present. The King gave a a signal to the Lord Mayor, who approached and knelt upon the lower step of the dais. Then his Majesty borrowed a sword from Lord Stanley, and, tapping the chief magistrate lightly on each shoulder, bade him rise. I The new Knight—for such he was now—regained his feet and kissed his Majesty's extended hand. At length the great new dock (No. 9) in the canal at Salford was rese,hed. It is 2,800 ft. long, and has f4ft. depth of water. OPENING TFIE NEW DOCK. The opening ceremony was very simple. The King drew a small lever at a table in front of him, which caused an electric circuit to become closed ; and, there- upon, a boom across the entrance to the dock fell, and I disappeared beneath the water. His Majesty immedi- ately declared the dock to be open a royal salute was Ifired; and some steamers, heavily laden with passengers, I commenced to pass in. I Later in Peel Park the King received an address from ' the Mayor and Corporation of Salford and unveiled a memorial to Lancashire Fusiliers who fell in the South African war. The Kiag during his visit reviewed some Crimean veterans, and a company of Navy League boys. The Queen accepted bouquets from a blind girl and from a docker's daughter. Their Majesties reached Victoria station shortly before five o'clock, and with a hearty sead-off returned to Knowsley. Alderman Jonas, Lord Mayor of Sheffield, has re- ceived a telegram from Lord Knollys stating the King proposes to confer upon him a knighthood.

cries of children. He forced.open.the door of the house
and found the male defendant fighting with his married daughter. The female defendant was lying on the floor bleeding from the mouth and the children were screaming with fright.

div.head: LATE REV. R. GREENALL.
div.p: THE LATE REV. R. GREENALL.
Funeral at Grappenhall.

The remains of the late Rev. Richard Green,'ll, for many years Rector of Grappenhall, were interred in the Grappenhall Churchyard on Saturday amid general manifestations of regret. A special service was held at noon in St. Wilfrid's chinch which was conducted by the Revs. H. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, the Rev. H. V. Pigot, vicar of St. Thomas's Stockton Heath and the Curate of Grappenhall. the Rev. E. E. Farrar. There was a large congregation present. As the congregation dispersed the organist played the Dead March in "Saul." The service at the graveside was conducted by the Rev. H. V. Pigot. The grave was lined with evergreens and choice white flowers and the double oak coffin, bore the following incription :—" Richard Greenall, M.A., born 2nd March, 1f330, died sth July, 1905." Carved into the oak top were the words : " I have kept the faith." A muffled peal was rung during the morning. The chief mourners were the Misses Greenall (daughters), Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. and Mrs. H. Greenall. Mr. Cyril Greenall, and Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Jones. Others nresent included the Rector of War- rington (the Rev. Canon Willis), the Rector of Winwick (the Rev. Canon Penrhyu). the Rector of Lymm (the Rev. G. B. Thurston). the Rev. 11. B. Blom E. C. E. ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn, on Wednesday, a watercress seller named Thomas Jannion was charged with assaulting Mrs. Ann Woodfine, keeper of the model lodging house. On Monday he knocked her down with his fist, causing her to bleed inwardly and giving her a black eye. The prisoner had forty-three previous convictions for various offences. He wr,s sentenced to two months' hard labour.

Mr. Gough: Yes. I say no more should be done. The Borough Treasurer: Mr. Gough has said money has been improperly used. I should like to know his definition of" improperly used." Mr. Gough: Extras paid for what had not been authorized, and the architect would not give a certifi- cate for.

Mr. E. England said he spoke on behalf of 200 of the largest ratepayers in Warrington. He was gratified with the way the inquiry had been carried out. He wished to' inform the Inspector that they in Warrington did not speak of these buildings as the Police Buildings, but more as the" Palace of Justice," because they had good reason to be proud of them from an architectural point of view. They were under the impression the buildings had cost them a little too much money, but at the same time he really thought they were under some misappre- hension. He was under the impression from the report of the last inquiry that it had been estimated that the buildings were to cost £19,000, and that a contract was entered into for that amount. Now they heard from Mr. Longdin that a deputation, after visiting various towns, advised the spending of £25,000 on the buildings and he was surprised now to find that the cost was 230,000. There was no doubt that the police buildings had caused much comment in the town, fairly and unfairly, and they would he very glad when the whole matter was settled. There had been a great deal of uneasiness in the minds of people and charges had been made in various ways. Whether they were true or not be could not ,ay; it was only by an inquiry of that kind that the truth could come to light The way Mr. Hindle had given his evidence was a credit to him, and many matters had been cleared up by him and the other officials. But what he wanted to know was:' "Why should the scheme cost another £50001" The Inspector: That is what I have been trying to , find out in this two days' inquiry. Mr. England : I don't for a moment allege the money has been iotproperly spent. We are all liable to mistakes. At the same time I think it would be wise when the Corporation go into these mitters at the nub et to allow for contingencies, and not exceed their estimates. Mr. England continuing said that the Coiport.tion continually exceed their estimates. Corporations never I appeared to go a few thousands under the mark; it was always a few thousands over. If the Inspector thought I fit not to allow certain items in the amount asked for I then itwas possible the charge would come upon the I borough rates for sue year, which they all felt would ' boa hardship. They were sufficiently burdened in War- rington already, and he would ask the Inspector to I recommend that if the noard disallowed any items the time for payment might be expended. The Inspector said that if the Board decided to die. I allow items, they simply struck them off, and it was for the Council to raise the money in their own way. Councillor Pemberton said they had not gone into certain matters before the public regarding the Police! Station, because he thought the Inspector would not allow it.

The Inspector, in closing the inquiry, intimated that there might be some delay as the plans would have to go before the Home Office. He would make out his report in due course, and the Local Government Board would communicate with the Town Council.
During the afternoon the Inspector visited the police buildings.

div.head: Daresbury Petty Sessions
div.p: Daresbury Petty Sessions
TUESDAY. Before Messrs. W. (2 Jones (presiding), H. Neild and
H. M. Edelsten.

THEFT OF A HEN.—Thomas Barlow and John Aspinall (two youths) were charged with having stolen a hen at Grappenhall, on July 6tb, of the value of 35., the property of Mr. J. Charlton Parr.—Prisoners pleaded guilty.—William Hewitt. farm bailiff, in the service of Mr. Parr proved the case.—Mr. Browne, who appeared for the prisoners, stated that they bore good characters, and he asked the Bench to take that into consideration. —The Chairman said the Bench did not like to make gaol-birds of people if they could possibly help it. The prisoners would be let off on that occasion and would simply be bound over to appear if called upon to do so. EMBEZZLEMENT AT STOCKTON HEATH.— Harry Deakin, of Stockton Heath, was summoned for having on the 10th June stolen the sum of £1 3s. 10d., the moneys of Messrs. R. White and Sons, Limited.—De- fendant pleaded guily.—Mr. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the firm, and stated that they were large mineral water manufacturers and did business through- out the country. They had an establishment at Stockton Heath where the defendant was employed as a traveller and he earned good wages and commission. He turned up on the date named and admitted that he was short of £1 3s. 10d., which he had spent. The principal object of the firm was to put a stop to others tampering with money. The magistrates had recently had before them two other cases of pensioners, and as it was thought the pensions might be lost if a conviction took place, which would be out of all proportion to the offence, the prisoner. had been discharged. Deakin was a respectable man.— The magistrates decided to inflict a fine of 10a. and costs.—Mr. Browne stated that in the case of Alfred Lamb, who was charged with embezzlement at the previous court, the offence was a pensioner and he would lose £7 a quarter for embezzling £5 odd. With the permission of the previous chairman (Mr. j.C.Parr) it was decided to take an adjournment of the case to enable the prisoner to resume his work. That had been done, and it was found that the prisoner had done his duty satisfactorily and was still acquitting him- self in a satisfactory manner. He asked for the case to be withdrawn. The magistrates consented to that course being adopted.

I am very pleased to find that the number of members in the Children's Corner is increas- ing. Bear in mind that the hundredth will receive a prize volume, so send on your name at once. Will the four last members please let me know their ages; their names are Nellie Keene, Harold Hoose, Reginald Coote, and George Carpenter, as otherwise I cannot award them prizes? I have received a very nice letter from Lily Hodgson. and, she tells me that the puzzles were very difficult; but try again, as the more you do the easier it will become. I expect to re- ceive a number of letters during this month, as you will remember I offered a prize to the one who wrote me the best letter. Well now, try your very best, and tell me what you are doing; write to me just the same as if you were talking. Good-bye for the present I hope you will all spend very pleasant holidays, as I expect you will all be having them at the end of this month.
Your affectionate UNCLE NED.

div.head: SEAWEED IN KIDNEY DISEASES.
div.p: SEAWEED IN KIDNEY DISEASES.
ALSO 50 PRIZE VOLUMES
STANLEY'S MAO IC BOOK (Continued).

"The stranger's words are not straight!" answered the savage, fiercely. "Did we not see him making spells of witchcraft against us, and drawing them on the magic charm that he carries with him'?" A sudden light flashed upon Stanley—it was his note-book that had offended them. "If the white chief means fairly by us, let him throw his magic work into yonder fire, and then he shall be our brother, and shall eat with us; but if not, our spears shall reach his heart!" A ferocious growl from the rest, and a siGnifi- cant brandishing of spears and bows, added fresh point to this last remark. For one moment the bold traveller stood aghast. To destroy his valuable notes, gathered with so much toil and suffering, would be to fling away the whole fruit of his weary and perilous journey! Yet, to refuse miplit cost his life and the lives of all his men, for the savages were evidently in earnest, and all the thickets around him were already swarming with fierce faces and levelled weapons. What was 19 be done?

All at once a bright idea came to him. In his pouch lay a small pocket Shakespeare (the companion of all his wanderings), which was sufficiently like the objectionable note-book to have deceived a keener observer than an African savage. Quick as thought he drew it forth, and held it up so that everyone could see it. "Is this the charm that. my brothers wish me to burn?" he asked, loud enough to be heard by all present.

"It is! it is!" roared a hundred voices at once, while half.a-dozen bony, black bands were outstretched from the front rank of the crowd as if to clutch the formidable "witch-book." "And if I burn it," said Stanley, "will you be friends with me, and give food to my men?"

div.p: "We will," chorused the black spearmen.
"Behold, then!" cried the great leader, and with one jerk.of his hand he flung the Shakes- peare into the fire beside him. In a moment it flamed up, shrivelled away, and was gone!

4. Then broke forth a yell of delight from the superstitious savages, as they saw the dreaded " magic " vanish into smoke. A score of big, bare-limbed warriors, all smeared with paint and grease, rushed forward to overwhelm their "white brother" with sticky embraces, while others brought forward armfuls of fruit, fish, and potato-like cassava bread. Stanley's hungry men ate their fill, and all went as merrily as a picnic. ,

Many a night after, while struggling wearily along the windings of the unknown river, the great explorer missed the book that had been his companion in so many perils and sufferings. But the precious notes were saved, and the narrative which they formed has since been read and applauded from one side of the world to the other.
A JULY DAY.
West wind that ruffles the sea into laughter and sparkle and spray; Skies blue as they can be; white clouds across
the bay; And a thistle seed sailing over a field of blossoming clover,— That is a July clay I

div.head: WHAT THE BUTCHER BOY SAID..
div.p: WHAT THE BUTCHER BOY SAID..

The question concerning the butcher boy, the dead pigeon, and the g,arde..er, which was put to the readers of the "Children's Corner" a fele weeks ago, has not been exactly solved by &Hy of the guesses at what the boy said, although we have received answers from many young friends, two or three of whom have made gueesea which differ only in detail from what was really said.

It will be remembered that the. pigeons were seen sunning themselves on the barn in a. wealthy mail's house-yard, wuien was preside.i over by a gardener of feec-rsious aspect anti terrible reputation among the boys of that neigh- bourhood. The butcher boy was seen to approach on a neighbouring' side-walk; to dis- cover the pretty birds; to drop his basket; to draw his bean-shooter, and to kill one of the birds. After that, he walked across the street and rattled the garden gate. The feeocions gardener came, and, after listening to what the boy said, went away and, bringing the dead. pigeon, presented it to the boy, who walked oil whistling light-heartedly. Subsequent inquiry has shown that the boy was in one important respect better than boys usually are who delight in frightening, maim- ing, er killing helplesscreatures, and that the case was otherwise peculiar. "Mister," said the boy to the gardener, "I have hurt one of your pigeons. I ti:d not mean to. I fired my bean-shooter, and thought it would only scare them; but one pigeon fell, and I am afraid it is killed. I have six shillings saved up, and I will pay for it gladly, if you will take the money." "Bless me!" exclaimed the gardener; "you are the first boy I ever saw who did not take to his heels when he had done wrong. The pigeons, though they belong to us are great nuisances; and if you had killed ;hem all, it would have pleased my boss. But, my boy, killing and hurting hapless things, because they are smaller and weaker than you are, is bad business; and if you had- not been so honest, I would. have thought you had a wicked heart. Let me give you the pigeon to take home." Ile went and ,g ot the pigeon. "There, now; take it, and show-it to your mother, and see what. she'll say. See if she does not tell you to throw away that bean-shooter. It is not a fit play- thing for an honest lad." One moral that may be drawn from this tale is, that the fierceness of a gardener seems to depend upon the conseiencts, rather than the eyes, of the boys who look upon him.
Perhaps other morals maybe found in it. Sr. NICHOLAS.

div.head: SEE-SAW.
div.p: SEE-SAW.
Tilt away, my little men, Out on Grandpa's lawn again; Jack is up, and Fred is down, It makes one laugh, the other frown,— Like our changeful summer weather.
"Well, never mind, just tilt it back, Up comes Fred and down goes Jack! Up and down, this is the way The sport goes on, the livelong day, When two little boys would tilt together."

div.p: BY THE CLUBMAN.
The Union Championships.

After a lapse of twelve years the Gosforth track at Newcastle was again the scene of an N.C.U. championship meeting on the 24th june. Some 8,000 spectators witnessed the 5 and 25 miles championships. In both eases the holders sus- tained their titles against all comers. Leon Mere- dith won the 5 miles by 2 lengths, and by a similar margin A. E. Wills secured the 25 miles. The short distance championships—the quarter, one mile, and one mile tandem—will take place on 29th July at Aston track, Birmingham, when, no doubt,' J. S. Penyon and H. D. .I.3ack will figure prominently. The attractions of the racing will be supplemented, as far as the Union officials are concerned, by a reception at the Birmingham Cyclists' Club House, and a motOr car trip to Kenilworth and Stratford- en-Avon on the Sunday. While referring to the Union, it is interesting to note that the financial result of Cycling's ' race meeting in May was a net profit of over £6O, which will go to swell the Union funds.

div.head: Discouragement of the Motorist.
div.p: The Discouragement of the Motorist.

It is only natural that motorists should view with misgiving the growing signs of public disapproval of their existence. The latest check administered is the exclusion of motor cars of every description from Hyde Park during certain hours in the after- noon. It is but a few years back since cyclists were similarly treated; but after a time the hard- ship was removed, so that to-day the cyclist has a free run of the park at all hours. A few weeks ago the Hon. John Scott Montague, M.P., inaugurated the "Considerate Driving League." The latest body of motor road users is styled "The Automobile Association," and has for its objects the protection and advancement of the legitimate interests of motorists, and in particular to assist in the enforce- ment of the laws affecting all users of the high- way. It is to be hoped that public opinion may exert a chastening effect upon the drivers of cars; but there is every indication that motorists will fight hard for the continuance of the present un- satisfactory state Of things. A study of the special papers devoted to the interest of motorists does not give a favourable impression of the sincerity of the talk about considerate driving, as far as the great majority of motorists are concerned.

div.head: Advertising for a Companion.
div.p: Advertising for a Companion.

Every touring season one encounters in the Cycling journals, more particularly in the 'Gazette,' the advertisements of cyclists needing a companion on a prospective tour. The writer has never known any one who advertised or answered an advertise- ment of this kind, but the obvious inquiry which arises is—Why do not these riders in quest of company join a club? By so doing they would find facilities for discovering congenial companions, and thus avoid the discomforts attendant on a hastily selected fellow-traveller, of possibly incom- patible tastes. The Club member also learns to avoid

div.head: PROMISCUOUSLY MADE FRIENDSHIPS
div.p: PROMISCUOUSLY MADE FRIENDSHIPS
in favour of the more carefully selected acquaint- anceship of fellow club members, about whom Gae generally has the opportunity of gaining know- ledge before embarking on a lengthened journey.

div.head: Common Danger.
div.p: A Common Danger.

The 'lrish Cyclist' points out what is a common source of danger to cyclists. It appears that carters are in the habit of placing large stones behind their waggon wheels, when resting their horses on steep bills, and these obstructions are often left in the road, where after nightfall they become a danger to cyclists. Any one encounter- ing obstacles of this sort should report the matter to the police or the highway authorities.

div.head: Results of the Hill Climb.
div.p: Results of the Hill Climb.

The Catford C.C. cannot complain of any lack Of support in their open hill climbing competition at Westerhain. Of the 61 entries no fewer than 46 cyclists rode up the bill. The entrants did not embrace many old performers, and F. S. Bate, last Year's winner, who was expected to break record, Proved a, disappointment. F: W. Wells, of the Brookdale C.C., a. former winner, also failed to score conspicuously, though his club furnished A. Garton, who made the fakteSt time up the hill, 4 in. (ta sec. The handicap was won by R. Barn- father, who rode a featherweight bicyle built of racing fittings, weight 181 b., geared to only 6514, evith 6i. cranks. Garton's mount was geared to 71 with 7 in. cranks. Only one Competitor had 8 in. cranks, his machine being a 39 lb. I oadster, and he made no show in the handicap, despite a liberal Start allowed him. The hill was in splendid con- dition.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

CHARRED REMAINS FOUND AT GLASSWORKS FURNACE. George McCrae, a workman at the glassworks of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, St. Helens, was looking for a leakage of water between two furnaces on Sunday when he came across the charred remains of a; man. The upper portion of the body was entirely destroyed, and portions of the legs below the knee alone remained. The ashes and remains were carefully collected and re- moved to the mortuary at the Town-t-lalLbut they were in such a condition that identification is practically im- possible. The place where the remains were discovered is usually instensely heated when the furnaces are in operation, and on Saturday night workmen noticed that something was smouldering between the furnaces. A hose-pipe was brought to bear upon vk hat was cousid- ied to be a small heap of rubbish, and the fire was extinguished. LORD TOLLEMACHE'S MOTOR INJURES AN EARLESEOWN LAD i' CYCLIST.

On Sunday Lord and Lady Tollemache, with their chauffeur, were proceeding from Teddington Hall to Dumfries in their motor car. On passing Hermitage Green-lane, Winwick, near Warrington, his lordship who aas driving, went on the wrong side of the road in attempting to steer clear of.l dog, and collided into a young lady cycling in the opposite direction, The cyclist, Miss Naylor, daughter of Mr. P. Naylor, land- lord of the Prince of Wales Hotel, Ear lestown, was brought down heavily. She was en route to Manchester to spend a few days with friends. Lord and Lady Tolle- mache did all in their power to aid Miss Naylor, ob- taining the attendance of Dr. Harrison, or Newton-le- Willows, and having her removed home on the horse ambulance. Miss Naylor was rendered unconscions,and is suffering from severe bruises and shock. Her machine was badly damaged.

RUNCORN WOMAN IN TROUBLE.— On Wednesday, at Runcorn, Mary Jane Schofield, a married woman, of Wellington-street, was charged with having, on the Ist inst., attempted to commit suicide by taking laudanum. It appeared from a statement by her hatband, Thomas Schofield, that she had been poorly for two years with ulcerated throat and mouth.—Janey Wells servant at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, deposed that she met her mother in Lord-street. They went into Duke's field, and while sitting on the grass her mother pulled the bottle produced out of her pocket, but she did not see her drinking any of the contents. The prisoner con- sented to be bound over for six months, and she was set at liberty, her husband promising to take care of her.
