div.head: VELOCITIES OF EXPLOSIONS.
div.p: THE VELOCITIES OF EXPLOSIONS.

Explosive mixtures are formed by glees that produce flame, and the velocity of the explosion waves in tubes has been shewn in late experiments by Professor Dewar. The maximum velocity seems to correspond with the motions cf the gas molecules. It was calculated in one case to be 105 miles per minute, at a given high temperature, and the atoms of the sir we breathe are supposed to be moving ordinarily about sixty times as fast as un express train.

div.head: SERPENT VENOM.
div.p: SERPENT VENOM.

One of the most curious things about serpent venom is that each species seems to be immune to its own poison. If a snake is inoculated with its own venom it remains unaffected. M. C. Phisalix, who has done so much work on this subject, finds experimental evidence that this immunity is to be attributed to the presence in the blood of a free antitoxin. This neutralises the poison as it is introduced.

div.head: ONE – PIECE RAILWAY WHEEL.
div.p: A ONE - PIECE RAILWAY WHEEL.

A process for making a one-piece steel railway wheel has been devised. For a 33in. wheel an ingot about 16in, in diameter is used, and with steam hammer and hydraulic press the ingot is forged until the hub and web are brought to practically the finished size. It is then subjected to a process of heat treatment, so that the outer portion of the wheel is brought to a roll- ing heat, while the web and hub are kept at a lower red heat. The rolling, process brings the wheel to its final shape.

div.head: COLOURING OF BIRDS' FEATHERS.
div.p: COLOURING OF BIRDS' FEATHERS.

In the spring all have noticed the deeper crimson that comes upon the robin's breast, as well as the new crest of the lapwing. The gerieral impression is that the spring brightening up is due to the growth of new feathers. But it has been pointed out at the Ornithological Congress that it is not always ro. In certain American birds, for example, the brighter colour is actually due to the wearing down of the feathers. The brightly-coloured barbs are covered with duller shaded barbules. When these latter weir off then the brighter spring plumage appears.

div.head: FEEDING GUINEA-PIGS ON POISONS.
div.p: FEEDING GUINEA-PIGS ON POISONS.

A French scientist, Dr. Carnot, has been experi- menting with different poisons upon guinea-pigs. Contrary to popular belief, he finds that certain poisons are fattening. Arsenic, phosphorus, and alcohol are decidedly stimulating. A guinea-pig weighing 11b. loz., which was given a milligramme of arsenic a day, doubled its weight in four months. Phosphorus administered in small doses produced a most gratifying effect, rendering the animal fat and sleek in a short space of time. Even lead, morphine, and strychnine—dangerous agents when taken in excess—gave gratifying results when taken in small doses daily. It appears, comments the Globe, that mankind i-lso thrives on poisons The best medicines are full of them, and sick people, leave their beds well and strong after being dosed with strong prescriptions of poison.

div.head: GOLD INSIDE NATURAL DIAMONDS.
div.p: GOLD INSIDE NATURAL DIAMONDS.

The origin of the diamond, the hardest and in some ways the most remarkable of minerals, is ono of the perplexing problems of geology. The idea has been held that great heat played an im- portant part in its formation, and M. Moissan has confirmed this theory by causing. small diamonds to crystallise out from fused Iron on suddenly cooling the surface of the latter. Some recent observations, however, seem to indicate that such crystals have formed at ordinary temperatures, ,growing to large size, like ordinary water-deposited crystals. For instance, ap.ophyllite, a silicate of lime and potash con. taming 16 per cent, of water, and easily fused by the blow-pipe, has been found inside a diamond, and gold also has been reported as an enclosure in the centre of a crystallised Brazilian stone.

div.head: SOUNDS FROM THE OCEAN DEPTHS.
div.p: SOUNDS FROM THE OCEAN DEPTHS.

An important advance in deep-sea surveying. saving much of the labour of present methods, is claimed for the acoustic sounding of M. Berg- graff, a Norwegian engineer. The depth is estimated from the time taken by sound to travel to the bottom and back, the echo from 2,000 ft. being received in one second, and the apparatus consists of a transmitter, an acoustic receiver, and a chronometer. The transmitter is a slowly revolving disc which at each revolu- tion closes an electric circuit and energises a magnet op,erating a vibrating armature. At each contact a sound is sent to the bottom of the sea, and the vibrations are tuned to the only pitch to which the specially constructed re- ceiving microphone will respond. In accurate work, the time of contact and that of the return of the sound are registered with great precision on the revolving drum of a chronograph.

div.head: ARTIFICIAL MOUNTAIN FOLDS.
div.p: ARTIFICIAL MOUNTAIN FOLDS.

Lord Avobury has been carrying on some inte- resting experiments on mountain building, and has boon describing his results to the Geological Society. His apparatus enabled him to com- press a mass of 2ft. square superficial area to one of 22in. square by pressure in two direc- tions at right angles to each other. Miniature mountains were thus thrown up in which- many of the natural features of mountain chains were reproduced. There were folds and fractures and overthrusts in thew pigmy mountains, as there are In Nature's giants. In the Bristol coalfields, and more markedly in those of Belgium, the same seam, or set of seams, is often passed through several times in a single shaft. And in Lord Aveburv's artificially-folded strata a boring would pass through two, or even four, layers of the same substance.

div.head: 10,000 HORSE-POWER TURBINE.
div.p: A 10,000 HORSE-POWER TURBINE.

Two steam turbine seta of 10,000 horse-power each, installed at the Ithenanian-Westphalian elec- tricity works, are the largest turbine sets, and in fact the largest stationary engines, of all Europe. Fisch of these gigantic ongioes comprises a turbine running at 1,030 r. p. nl., which is direct-connected to a rotary current generator of 5,000 kilowatts, 5,000 volts, and 50 periods per second. as well as to a direct•current generator ot 1,500 kilowatts and 600 volts, end to a central condensing plant. The whole set is 20 metres in length, and weighs 190 tons, of which 9.4 metres and 107 tons correspond to the turbine. The maximum height of the turbine above the floor is 2-6 metres, and the maximum breadth likewise 2.6 metres. The turbine is of the single-cylinder type, and has only two bearings, one of whb h serves at the same time as a bearing t.) the alternator. The governor is made to corn- p-nsate to 1 per cent, for any oscillations in the i angular speed, with variations n the load as high as 20 per cent., while the maximum variation in the number of revolutions between running at no load and at full load is not to exceed 5 per cent. Another unit of the same size is shortly to be installed at the power station in a Westphalian mining company.
The Examiner, Saturday, July 15, 1905.

div.head: Pity the Rabbits!
div.p: Pity the Rabbits!

Sir,—As your columns are always open to an appeal on behalf of the helpless and suffering may I be allowed to direct the attention of landownersto the cruelty now being practised on sortie estates. We can scarcely blame Continentals for their occasionntreferences to our smug hypocrisy and callousness to all suffering except the particular brands which are peculiar to other people. But if the facts were known and appreciated I think landowners would soon abolish a custom which is a stain on the English race. They are by repute kind-hearted men, and in their case as with all of us " evil is wrought for want of thought." The writer and another were by chance near some rabbit holes. On looking down one we saw an iron trap holding a rabbit about six weeks old by the skin and breast bone. Its struggles and evident pain and terror were pitiable. Looking down another hole we saw another held by both forelegs. The bones were broken and it was tugging at the connecting skin in its efforts for freedom. Many other holes were near but, although seasoned men who have seen much o f the seamy side of life, the sights were too sickening to investigate further. This was within sound of the chimes of at least a dozen churches where multitudes gather to worship the common Father who " feeds the ravens yea providently caters for the sparrow." We naturally recoil from the horrors of the bull 'ring but is there anything in that comparable with the acute and prolonged suffering of a trapped rabbit ? It cannot be excused the excitement of snort which in this case does not exist ; nor by necessity. for they could be des- troyed by more humane methods ; nor even in the cause of science. As far as my experience goes the laboratory rabbit is a favoured animal in comparison with these. It is probable that an appeal to humane feeling will be enough in many cases, but electors may be reminded they are responsible for laws which allow such cruelty, and an effort should be made to promote legis- lation which would make trapping a statutory crime:lf its terrible nature were once realised, there would be an outcry which could not be disregarded. It is stated that the King has prohibited trapping on his estates. If true it is what we should expect from his previous record, and I sincerely hope his example may be speedily and universilly followed.—Yours, Sze., PAGAN.

Sir, it is "a practical system of unive•al training " which the National Service League urges upon the people of Great Britain. Let us have done with I platitudes and fetishes and look facts fair and square ;in the face. "if we intend to maintain the integrity of ' this Empire. which means the prosperity of Great Britain, we must accept the responsibilities of such a charge." Let us remember that no Government can be expected officially to support a noble appeal for national duty such as that made by Lord Roberts unless the people themselves show that they are ready to respond. And there is no surer way of helping the great soldier who has rendered such signal services to the country than by joining the National Service I Leanne and thus forming that body of public opinion to which a patriot statesman can appeal. This I earnestly ; invite your readers to do without delay. I have the honour to be, your obedient servant, RAGLAN, President. The National Service League, Dacre Elousa, Victoria-st., S.W. div.head: Has Preaching Degenerated Into a Trade?
div.p: Has Preaching Degenerated Into a Trade?

Sir.—On the 24th of June, it was reported that, in a sermon dealing with clerical incomes, the Bishop of Burnley said, "In all sobriety he ventured to offer a counsel of despair. Cancel all canons against the clergy engaging in worldly occupations. Let one-half of their time be occupied in some honest trade, that the other half might he set free for the operations of the heart at leisure from itself, and a mind uncrusted by ceaseless worry." The reference here to canon law reminds me that the ministers of the State Church are, for some reason or other, prohibited from employing any portion of their time in secular pursuits. But this rule, like many other ecclesiastical arrangements, has no founda- tion in the Gospel code which was specially designed to direct the faith and practice of all believers in Christ. I therefore most heartily endorse the Bisnop's recommendation to rescind the canon that the clergy may be free to labour like other honest men ; and I would extend it to the salaried ministers of all other denominotions. The highest precedents in New Testa- ment history aro in favour of this course, and none against it. The purest, the noblest, and the infinitely greatest Preacher that the world has ever seen, or ever will see, was Jesus the founder of Christianity. And yet he laboured for many years as a carpenter in the Vale of Nazareth before he ventured upon his wonderful mission as the Saviour of the world. Nay more. From the fact that during the whole of his brief ministry he was known and recognised as " the Carpenter" I am inclined to infer that even then he had not altogether abandoned the occupation of his early days. Be this as it may, we know that He was sent forth to be our example in all things ; and if He laboured with His hands it was to show His followers in all ages that they should devote themselves to some useful manual employment. For work, when performed as in the sight of God, imparts a dignity to human beings which nothing else can do. And here I may observe, parenthetically, that it is only the poverty of their faith in His Almighty power which prevents Christians from imitating His miracles too. Then the Apostles were all working men, chosen by the Lord as fittest to represent him in the world when he had gone. And during the whole of their ministry they laboured with their own hands to provide for their wants lest they should entail any charge on their followers. They might indeed, have claimed to live by trio Gospel, as the Jewish priests had lived by the offer- ings of the Temple, but they chose a nobler and more independent course, and one more in keeping with the spirit and usage of their master. Besides, they knew that if they had sold their services for money they would have become the servants of their paymasters, and not of God. Their liberty would have been sacrificed and a precedent founded for the wolves in sheep's cloth- ing who, in after years, would creep into the church to make merchandise of the souls of men. And when the Apostles had passed away other but less gifted men were raised up to continue the work, who supported themselves and their families by their usual avocations. Even as late as the middle of the second century, Polycarp, a pupil of " the beloved disciple," in his Epistle to the Philippians, charges the presbyters (elders or overseers) to provide for that which is be- coming in the sight of God and men. But the working-ministry of the Gospel gradually died out, and was succeeded by a mercenary system wholly at variance with the principles of Christianity. This system received a tremendous impetus early in the fourth century, when the Emperor Constantine, set himself up as the head of the Church, and proceeded to endow it upon a most elaborate scale. In the man- made-church thus founded we have the oriqin of the English establishment of religion. Like Constantine, King E d ward is the head of the church, ruling through a Hierarchy rich in salaries varying from £1,500 to .£15,000 a year, and adorned with titles which the Gospel only mentions to condemn, nor can I acquit the so- called Free Churches of the love of money and honours It is well known that all the preachers are at least " Reverend," and that the popular ones can and do com- mand large stipends, while less known men must no content with smaller remuneration. The standards upon which the respective valuations are made is, of course, private and pertains to the various finance committees. And the natural outcome of the whole stipendiary system is that we have much formalism and little real chris- tianity for the millions expended every year upon preaching and other methods. Ihe one and only remedy for this unsatisfactory state of things is to revert to the purity and simplicity of primitive times. When it is found that the Gospel ministry does not yield a life of learned ease and com- fort, but entails toil, self-denial and suffering there will be a change for the better ; the mercenaries will gradually disappear, and the faithful shepherds alone will remain. And their place will not be with the rich and the learned, but among "the poor of this world rich in faith, and heros of the kingdom which God bath promised to them that love him." (James ii-5.)---Yours truly lONA.

Religious Instruction. Sir,.—l desire to thank Mr. Dormice for writing of me in such kind and generous terms. I am not anxious to continue this correspondence because I feel that the range of the subject is becoming so extended that too much of our time as well as of your space will be taken up by discussing it so exhaustively. At the same time I do not think it courteous to Mr. Dunnleo to leave his letter without any reply. I will therefore once more ask for some of your space and then—so far as I am concerned—this correspondence must cease. Let me endeavour to bring our discussion back to its original line of thought. In preaching to a Church of England congregation on behalf of their schools I endeavoured to show that the Church of England had done much for elementary education in the past and that we of the present should follow this good example. I date the beginning of this work from the foundation of the Charity Schools at the latter end of the 17th Century. I do not say that the system was an ideal one but I do say that it was the first step in caring for the education of the poorer classes in the country. Mr. Dnnnico sneaks of a paltry 500 but this is a curious under-statement. By 1741 the S.P.C.K. alone had founded 2,000 and this by no means represents the whole number. I feel that Mr. Dunnico has failed to shake this position. After the ISth Century we come to the work of the National Society. This I maintain was a development of the work of the S.P.C.K. In proof of this I may refer Mr. Dunnico to the authoritative histories of those two societies in which he will find this clearly stated. He refers me to a statement of Earl Russell's. I must decline to attach historical importance to political utterances, made for a political purpose. I take my stand upon the charters and original documents of the societiesond I retain my opinion. I quite allow that the action of the National Society was quickened and intensified by that of the British and Foreign School Society. The members of the Church of England then, as now, desired to teach their children the truths they held dear. If to do this is to be" narrow," then we must accept the title. As regards the cost of building schools I still main- tain that, with all due allowance for Government grants and for contributions made by companies and others for the purpose of keeping out School Boards, large and generous contributions have been given by the different religious bodies in the past. For these contributions the present generation owes them a debt of gratitude which it ought to pay by a sympathetic consideration for the opinions of the donors. With regard to Mr. Boucher's book the facts so far as I have been able to ascertain them do not tally with Mr. Dunnico's description and I have no doubt that at this distance of time it is difficult to discover exactly what did happen. But whichever of us is right, I must protest strongly against an obscure book of this kind being put forward as representing the teaching of the Church of England. It is easy to find books and pamphlets emanating from members of different denominations in which Passages occur that would be strongly repudiated by the denomination as a whole. This book has been publicly and solemnly repudiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury and it ought not to he quoted as if it were a text book in use. Mr. Dunnico does not know our schools or our teachers, otherwise he would not write as he does. If he will go into any Church school in Warrington and listen to the teaching he will find that it is no part of our object to stir up strife or to speak disrespect- fully of other Christian bodies. In conclusion, let us admit that we have all made mistakes in the past and let us clean the slate and set down the problem again. Upon the religious education of our children depends the future of our nation. On this we are all agreed. The problem is how to do this with --- due regard for the full liberty of religious belief. " SUCCESS TO THE fiRM Alderman Francomb in proposing this toast remarked that success seemed to follow the firm year by year. There were many things which contributed to that excellent state of affairs. In the first place they had the benefit of having gentlemen like Sir Peter Walker as chairman of the company, and Mr. John Reid Walker and Col. Hall Walker as managing directors, and it would be difficult indeed to find better men for the positions. (Hear, hear.) He did not think it was pos- sible to meet a more kindly gentleman than Sir Peter while Mr. John Reid walker and Col. Walker were two excellent men of business, and he was sure they all took a most lively interest in everything connected with the breweries and their employ4s, and were ever ready to help on any deserving man. Excellent masters he thought, resulted in their having excel- lent men, and in going about the breweries for about 28 years, he could say that the men from the highest to the lowest, all seemed to thoroughly accept their responsibilities. So far as the head officials were concerned it was impos- sible to find a more devoted body of workers, and as long as they did their duty in the way they had done it in the past, success was certain to follow. (ffear,hear.) That day there was a sort of gloom over them because of the absence of their dear friend, Mr. Monro. He had had a most serious illness, and he was sure they were all very well pleased indeed to know that he was rapidly improving. (Applause.) He saw him yesterday, and he thought he would be back again amongst them in a few weeks. They would have been delighted if he could only have been with them that day, but instead they hoped he was doing well in the forest near North- wich, where he had gone to stay for a time. In pro- posing the toast, he would couple with it the name of Mr. Parry, the head brewer, in whom Mr. now° had a devoted friend—(applanse)—and express the hops that Mr. Monro would soon be with them again. The toast was enthusiastically honoured. Is reply, Mr. Parry said it was pleasing to hear of the firm's continued success. and be could assure them that if only the employ& did their ditty, the directors would stand by them. (Hear, hear.) There were very few in that room, perhaps, who knew that as lately as last Thursday he made—or rather commenced—the first brow in their lately acquired Liverpool brewery. (Applause.) He could only hope—as they would all hope—that it would be attended with the same success as their War- rington brewery. He thanked them on behalf of the firm for the cordial way in which they had drunk the toast.

div.head: DAY AT BLACKPOOL.
div.p: A DAY AT BLACKPOOL.
Messrs. Peter Walker and Son's Trip.

To the average workingman few things present more I pleasant pictures than the prospect of a day's trip to some popular sea-side resort, and on Saturday some 90 works excursions visitel Blackpool. Not the least of these were alessrs.Peter Walker and Son's employees who are to be congratulated upon their selection of the famous Lancashire town as their destination. Their annual outing is a particularly enjoyable one as owing to the generosity of their employers all apprehension as to probable financial disability is removed. Each man is given two railway tickets, the day's wages is allowed mid a grant is made which allows the men to set out in a state of comparative affluence. Such facts in themselves are sufficient to ensure a day's enjoyment but on Saturday even the above list was incomplete as arrangements had been made for the trippers to be admitted free to the principal places of amusement which have made Blackpool famous. Under such circumstances he indeed must have been a morose individual who did not appreciate the holiday and one whom it would be practically impossible to please. Walkers workpeople are of a more cheery disposition and as everything to them was viewed through rose- tinted spectacles they spent the crowded day in most thorough enjoyment. Naturally there was some anxiety as to the probable state of the weather but the trippers on rising at an hour which to many was unusually early, were greeted with a flood of brilliant sunshine and they made their way to Bank Quay Station buoyed up with the prospects of an exceptionally fine day—though even less propitious weather could hardly have affected their spirits. They came from all points of the compass and the station presented an animated spectacle as the thousand trippers —to be minutely accurate the number was 1,201— exchanged friendly greetings. The first " special" was timed to leave at 6.15 and punctual to the minute it steamed out of the station carrying a cheering crowd. The remainder of the party set out on the journey some fifteen minutes later. Both trains were expresses and the fact was sarcastically emphasised when after three- quarters of an hour twelve miles had been travelled ! What was lacking in regard to speed early on the journey was, however, made up for later' Blackpool baing reached shortly before eight o'clock. It was then that the true Lancashire spirit displayed itself and the cheering trippers were almost too impatient to await the assembling of the band which headed them in their march into the town. The district is the reverse of being noted for the beauty of its surrounding on imme- diate scenery, and the trippers wasted no time vainly seeking for shady spots, but at once proceeded to dis- port themselves on the sands. Blackpool has earned the title of " breezy " but on Saturday it balled its name. To use a nautical expression there was barely a capful of wind, and in the blazing sunshine the only cool spot was on the seashore or in the sea itself—and the number who took a dip in the " briny " was by no means small. It is unnecessary to dilate upon Black- pool's artificial aids to enjoyment, save to say that they fulfilled their allotted purpose. The tower and its many attractions were visited, and the top of the tall struc- ture, reached by means of the lift, afforded an excellent view to thousands. The North Pier and the other recognized sights of the town were visited. In till afternoon the various enter- tainments received their fair share of patronage. It was a happy coincidence that Saturday should have been fixed for the opening of the great swimming con- tests and those interested in acquatic displays were well catered for. Others visited suburban villages and mot a few went on the " cars" to Fleetwood. There was no lack of anything to amuse and the time passed all too quickly and it is with regret that the trippers at 10 o'clock in the evening bade good-bye to the town which by general consent, had proved such an admirable choice for perhaps the most enjoyable outing ever held in connection with the firm.

SOME SPEECH MAKING. In the evening the staff and invited guests lined at the Hotel Metropole. an excellent repast being pro- vided. Councillor J. Fulton Smith presided, and amongst those present were Mr. A. F. G. Potter. Mr. Ernest Parry, Aldermen Francomb, Hutchinson and Smethurst, Councillor John Roberts, and other local gentlemen. After dinner various toasts were honoured, 1 the usual loyal toasts being heartily drunk.

div.p: FREE EDUCATION WANTED.

Mr. John Naylor Entertains the Warrington Club.
element, and were very successful in thair efforts to amuse. Mr. G. Finch was an able accompanist.

During an interval Mr. E. Pickavance proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. John Naylor for their hospitality. He said it had been his privilege for many years to perform that pleasant function, and he sincerely hoped they would all be spared for many years to meet at that picturesque spot. (Applause). Mr. Davies seconded, and paid a warm tribute to Mr. and Mrs. Naylor for their kindness to the club extend- ing over many years. He also feelingly alluded to the fact that since the last visit to Beeston Towers, the Hon. Secretary of the club had had the misfortune to lose both his fatherand eldest sister, and said that he was sure all the kindest sympathies of the members went out to him in his great bereavement. (Hear, hear). The motion was heartily agreed to. Mr. John Naylor, who was received with musical honours, thanked the club for the kind manner in which they had received him. He was proud to be president of such a club, and of all the visitors to Beeston none were more welcome than the members of the Warring- ' ton Cyclino. Club, and their lady friends. On behalf of himself, Mrs. Naylor and family, he thanked them and hoped for many years to come they would look forward to the annual visit to Beeston Towers. (Applause). The programme concluded with a dance, and the National Anthem having been sung,the wheelers started for home. The ride through Delamere Forest in the cool of the evening was a very pleasurable ending to one of the most successful outings in the history of the club.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH POTATO MARKET,
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH POTATO MARKET,
Action Taken by the Police.
TEST CASES FAIL.

Unusual interest was taken in the proceedings at Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday when thirteen well- known Cheshire farmers were summoned by the police for obstructing the free passage of a highway at Stock- ton Heath. The alleged obstruction arose in connection with the holding of the potato market in Victoria- square, Stockton Heath, and the gentlemen summoned were Albert kVhalley, Stockton-lane Farm, Latchford Without ; Harry Hi,ghfleld,Nfassey Brook Farm,Thelwall Charles Massey, the Hollies, Antrobus; Joseph Percival, Tanyard Farm, Appleton ; Ernest Wilkinson, Pool's Platt Farm ; Antrobus ; Thomas Moseley, Hill Farm, Antrobus: Edwin Jones, Moss Side Farm, High Legh ; Albert Weir, Barnet Farm, Hatton; Charles Lloyd, Birchall's Gorse Farm, High Legh ; Samuel Lloyd, Reed's SideXarna, Antrobus ; and John Lomas, 43, Viaduct- street, Earlestown. The obstruction was alleged to have been caused at various times during the afternoon of June 23rd. Mr. Browne appeared for all the defendants. It was arranged that one case should be heard as a test case. and the hearihg of the charge against Mr. Joseph Percival was proceeded with. Acting-Sergeant Bowyer stated that on the 23rd June he was on duty in Victoria-square when he saw defend- ant in charge of two horses and a lurry which was laden with potatoes and which were standing on the land opposite the Mulberry Tree Inn. Tnere was an obstruction of the highway. The lurry remained from 3.50 to 4.30. He spoke to the defendant and told him that he should report him. There was a public road at this particular spot, to two shops, and a thoroughfare to Gasket° street and other streets adjoin- ing. There was also a back way to the Police Station. As all the carts met together it was awkward for any- one to pass. He (the officer) had to remove some of the carts to enable other vehicles to pass through into Gaskele-street. .

Mr. Browne : I suppose this is a very grave case resoecting the Stockton Heath Council and the farmers? There was no answer. Mr. Browne : Was there any actual physical obstruction ? Witness : To the shops around Gaskele-street and the back of the Police Station. These carts have been there in the potato season for a number of years ?—Yes. sir. I have known them for 30 years and you will not con- tradict that ?—No, sir. I have witnesses who have ben there 55 years. You won't dispute that ?—No, sir. And the object is principally to put a stop to the market ?—No, sir. What is it then ?—To put an end to the obstruction. I Who is the instigator of these proceedings ?—I can not say. I suppose you received your instructions from Sergeant Barlow, and he from the Superintendent of the Police at Runcorn ? The Clerk (Mr. Hoary Greenall) : They came really and truly through the Chief Constable of the county. Mr. Browne : Is the Warrington Corporation behind 9.11. this ? The Sergeant : Not so far as I ern concerned. am told that in front of Mr. Porcival's two horses and lurry there was a cab standing : I did not see a cab. _ .

And a motor car ?—No, sir. There is a difference between farmers bringing potatoes to the Stockton Heath market and a cab and a motor? —I did not see any cab or motor car. Is there not ample room for horses, carts and lurries to any extent to go past ?—On the way to Grappenhall- road there is, but not through the thoroughfare I have mentioned. Have you inquired what number of yards in front of the Mulberry Tree belong to that inn ?—T asked Mr. Shillcock and he said he had inquired from the brewery peonle, but they could not answer the question. Unfortunately some of the members of the brewery belong to the Stockton Heath Parish Council, and there- fore, we are somewhat at a loss. There are cobble stones round the front ?—About three yards from the front. The Clerk: Is this a highway?—The public have access to it. They have a right to the stationer's shop; the butcher's shop and to the backway to the Police Station. The public have also a right to Gaskele-street. Sergeant Barlow stated that about ten of the carts were laden with potatoes. The obstruction took place on land which was in front of the Mulberry Tree. There was a road into Gaskele-street and to the back of the Police Station. The defendant in question had to remove his cart to allow another to go out of Gaskele- street into Victoria-square. Other carts had to be moved out of the way to enable the builders to take material to the Police Station. Mr. Browne: Really speaking is there any actual physical obstruction?—lf any one wants to pass to the shuns. This has been a potato market for many years.-1 have no reason to doubt that. These farmers have no object in view except to sell the potatoes ?—That is the purpose. And when they want to shoos their carts into those of the purchasers they go into the Mulberry Tree yard, and pay for the use of it ?—I cannot say that. Some have gone into the Mulberry Tree yard. They did not do so before. Mr. Browne said this was one of the most important cases that had ever been tried at Daresbury. Here they had a number of farmers of the highest respect- ability summoned for wilfully obstructing the highway The Bench had to take the word" wilfully "into con- sideration. What had happened? The farmers came down to Stockton Heath and brought their new potatoes, and dealers from Wigan, Ashton, Man- chester, and other places met them. There had been no objection to the market at least for 10 odd years, if not 55 years, until a few weeks ago, when a farmer was summoned, and he (Mr. Browne) represented him, and the summon 4 was dismissed. He submitted that the space in front of the Mulberry Tree Inn was not a high- way, but part of the curtilage of the inn. If that was so the Bench had no jurisdiction to try, and he claimed it. He said the horses' feet were on the cobble stones belonging to the Mulberry Tree, and they without doubt, belonged to the owners of the inn. Were the Bench going to be parties—he did not blame the police at all—to try to stop the farmers of the district selling their new potatoes at Stockton Heath ? That is what the prosecu- tion amounted to, obstruction or no obstruction. This market had been held so long—he had a witness who could speak for 55 years—that were the Bench to be parties to saying that the practice of holding it was illegal and must belput a stop to?:They quite knewwhere all this prosecution emanated from? It was a question of tolls, of a paltry 3d for which a certain Corporation wanted to drive these farmers in Warrington. But the greater convenience was at Stockton Heath. There the farmers had a canal traffic, and they could send their goods to Manchester at a little cost. What they said. and vary strongly, through him was this : First of all he claimed the right to stand on the Mulberry Tree yard. Having claimed that right on private grounds the jurisdiction of a Bench was ousted. If the Bench fou'nd against him on that point, what he said was that the market having existed so long they had the power under Lord Cross's Act—which he had often quoted—after hearing a charge for an offence punishable on summary iurisdiction, or if the offence in a particular case was of a nature so trivial that it was I inexpedient to inflict a punishment, to inflict a nominal penalty only. They might also dismiss the rinse without costs. He -(Mr. Browne) submitted that these farmers [ had been carrying on a market for years to the detri- ment of no One, and to the advantage of all. Therefore, he claimed a dismissal. He wished to say, in conclo- , sion, that not a single accident of any description had occurred during the whole of the 55 years the market had been in existence. The magistrates then retired to consider their decision, and on their return into Court, the Chairman said : The I Bench have given the matter very careful consideration . and have come to the conclusion that the farmers have , done their best to obviate what is undoubtedly a nuisance. „ We have decided to dismiss the cases, but we don't 5 allow Mr. Browne 's contention that they have a right to the ground around the Mulberry Tree. ' Mr. Browne: I accept your decision' Mr. Chairman, , and the difficulty will be obviated in future. It only I lasts for seven or eight weeks in the year.

Anniversary Services. The anniversary services in connection with the Baptist Church, Latchford, were held on Sunday when the pulpit was occupied morning, afternoon and evening by the Rev. J. W. Varley (St. Ann's-on-Sea), a former pastor of the church. A children's service was held in the morning when Mr. Varley delivered an address in the course of which he expressed the pleasure it afforded him once more to ho amongst his old friends. This, as well as Mr. Varlev's other discourses, was listened to' with interest. During the day Mr. Ernyln Davies, the celebrated Welsh vocalist, sang two solos in a charminfr manner, namely " Less of self" and "Channels only, while the choir were heard to considerable advantago in the anthems " Sing unto the Lord "and "Praise the Lord." Mr. Peter Harrison presided at the organ. The' collections, which were in aid of the general funds of the church, amounted to £l6 9s.
